A dollar-denominated withdrawable user balance is plain 'funds', and the governing provision for it is 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A). Use § 4.7 only for the CVC-denominated variant; do not let counsel be briefed on the wrong provision. NOT LEGAL ADVICE — get a written BSA analysis from US counsel before deciding you are outside this.

checklist.item: Written BSA/AML compliance programme: designated compliance officer, risk-based internal controls, ongoing employee training, independent testing
checklist.issuer: FinCEN / IRS Small Business & Self-Employed Division (the federal examiner for non-bank MSBs)
checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.prerequisite: MSB status determination
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1022.210. Registration alone is not compliance — the programme, not the form, is what examinations test.

checklist.item: Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing capability and procedures
checklist.issuer: FinCEN
checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.leadTime: Filing deadline is 30 calendar days after initial detection of facts constituting a basis for filing
checklist.prerequisite: AML programme; transaction monitoring
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1022.320. The dollar threshold for MSB SARs is UNVERIFIED — confirm the current figure in § 1022.320(a)(2) before writing it into procedures.

checklist.item: Currency Transaction Report (CTR) procedures
checklist.issuer: FinCEN
checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.leadTime: 15 days after the transaction (verify current deadline)
checklist.prerequisite: AML programme
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.311, transactions in currency over $10,000. Largely theoretical for a card/ACH-only app — CTRs cover physical currency — but the procedure must exist.

checklist.item: OFAC sanctions screening of users and payouts
checklist.issuer: Office of Foreign Assets Control, U.S. Department of the Treasury
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — any model that moves money
checklist.prerequisite: User identity data
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. Chapter V. Strict liability and applies to every US person regardless of MSB status. There is no registration — it is an operational control.

checklist.item: Register for the federal wagering occupational tax before accepting any wagers — IRS Form 11-C, 'Occupational Tax and Registration Return for Wagering'
checklist.issuer: Internal Revenue Service
checklist.appliesTo: B (likely); C only if counsel concludes entry fees are 'wagers' — see corrected analysis, which is now materially FAVOURABLE for an operator-funded fixed-prize contest
checklist.cost: $50 per year where the wager is authorised under the law of the state in which accepted; $500 per year otherwise (26 U.S.C. § 4411)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — must be filed before wagers are accepted
checklist.prerequisite: Determination (with counsel) whether entry fees are 'wagers' under 26 U.S.C. § 4421, AND a Fifth Amendment analysis — see below
checklist.notes: 26 U.S.C. §§ 4411, 4412. CORRECTED (audit defects 1 and 2): the original brief said 'skill-vs-chance is irrelevant here' and that the fixed-operator-funded-prize defence was untested with no authority in existence. Both are wrong. Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 holds that contesting for a prize offered by another in a contest of mental or physical skill, which the offeror must award in any event, is not gaming, and that an entry fee is not a wager 'unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'. AM 2020-009 (23 July 2020) discusses and endorses that ruling, and applied the tax to DFS specifically BECAUSE DFS entrants 'have no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players' — the opposite of a knowledge duel. AM 2020-009 is non-precedential (26 U.S.C. § 6110(k)(3)); Rev. Rul. 57-521 is a published revenue ruling and is citable. AUDIT ADDITION — FIFTH AMENDMENT (missing item 2): registering on Form 11-C at the $500 UNAUTHORISED rate is a public admission of accepting wagers not authorised under the law of the state where accepted, i.e. potential evidence of an 18 U.S.C. § 1955 / state gambling offence. Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968) and Grosso v. United States held the self-incrimination privilege a complete defence to prosecution for failure to register/pay the wagering taxes on the then-current scheme; the CURRENT scope of that privilege after subsequent statutory amendments is UNVERIFIED and must be settled with counsel BEFORE anyone files at the unauthorised rate. Do not file blind.

checklist.item: Monthly federal excise tax on wagers — IRS Form 730, 'Monthly Tax Return for Wagers'
checklist.issuer: Internal Revenue Service
checklist.appliesTo: B if entry/stake money is treated as wagers; C only if the Rev. Rul. 57-521 position fails
checklist.cost: 0.25% of the amount wagered if authorised under the law of the state in which accepted; 2% if not (26 U.S.C. § 4401(a))
checklist.prerequisite: Form 11-C registration
checklist.notes: 26 U.S.C. § 4401. The 2% rate on unauthorised wagers is applied to HANDLE, not revenue — at scale it can exceed gross margin. Model this before launch. CORRECTED FRAMING: this is a live and severe risk for MODEL B (player-v-player staking with a rake is the paradigm 'wagering pool ... conducted for profit', and the stake money alone comprises the prize — the exact Rev. Rul. 57-521 trigger). For MODEL C with an operator-funded, fixed, pre-announced prize NOT contingent on entrant numbers, the cited authority points the other way. The original brief's 'under-appreciated killer' framing was directionally wrong for Model C.

checklist.item: Prize and winnings information reporting and withholding (Forms W-2G / 1099-MISC; Form 945 for withheld amounts)
checklist.issuer: Internal Revenue Service
checklist.cost: 24% withholding rate under 26 U.S.C. § 3402(q) on certain net winnings of $5,000 or more
checklist.leadTime: Annual information returns; deposits per the withholding schedule
checklist.prerequisite: Collection of payee TIN (Form W-9) before payout
checklist.notes: For calendar year 2026 the minimum reporting threshold for certain information returns including Form W-2G is $2,000 (raised from $600 and inflation-indexed thereafter by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, enacted 4 July 2025; IRS/Treasury guidance published in the Federal Register 17 April 2026). Which of W-2G versus 1099-MISC applies to a knowledge contest is a real question for your tax counsel — it follows the same 'is this a wagering transaction' analysis as the excise tax. Separately, the same Act amended 26 U.S.C. § 165(d) to cap wagering-loss deductions at 90% of losses from the 2026 tax year. CORRECTED BILL NUMBERS (audit defect 10): the repeal bill is the FAIR BET Act, H.R. 4304 (119th Cong., Rep. Titus, introduced 7 July 2025) — NOT H.R. 6985, which the original brief cited and which could not be confirmed. The House Rules Committee declined to advance it as an NDAA amendment in January 2026 and it had not passed as of September 2026. The FULL HOUSE Act bill number 'S. 2230' remains UNVERIFIED. This is a player-facing communications issue, not an operator obligation.

checklist.item: COPPA compliance programme: neutral age screen before any personal information is collected, direct notice and verifiable parental consent for under-13s, COPPA-compliant privacy policy, data retention/deletion policy, strengthened security requirements
checklist.issuer: Federal Trade Commission
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — all models; unavoidable for a trivia product, which reads as child-attractive
checklist.prerequisite: Decide and document whether the service is child-directed, mixed-audience, or general-audience
checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. §§ 6501-6506; 16 C.F.R. Part 312. Amended Rule published 22 April 2025, effective 23 June 2025, FULL COMPLIANCE REQUIRED SINCE 22 APRIL 2026 — this is live law today, not a future deadline. Mixed-audience services must age-screen BEFORE collecting personal information, in a neutral manner that does not default to a set age or encourage falsification ('What is your date of birth?', never 'Are you over 13?'). The FTC's 'Enforcement Policy Statement Promoting the Adoption of Age-Verification Technology' of 25 February 2026 is confirmed to exist and is said to give limited relief for data collected solely to run age-verification technology — BUT ITS CONDITIONS AND SCOPE ARE UNVERIFIED IN THIS LANE (audit addition, missing item 5). A money model that hard-blocks under-18s depends on exactly that collection, so read the policy statement in full and confirm the conditions (permitted data categories, retention limits, whether it covers third-party vendors) before relying on it. Practical answer for any money model: hard-block under-18s entirely and document it — state minimum gambling/contest ages make under-18 money play indefensible regardless of COPPA.

checklist.item: FTC Act § 5 and Lanham Act disclosure and purchase-flow review: single-step purchase confirmation, no dark patterns, plain-language coin pricing, disclosure of any AI/bot opponents, disclosure of matchmaking logic, no account lockout for chargeback disputes
checklist.issuer: Federal Trade Commission (and, separately and more dangerously, COMPETITORS suing under the Lanham Act and state UDAP/GBL statutes)
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — all models, most acute for B and C
checklist.prerequisite: Final purchase and matchmaking UX
checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. § 45. Regulator benchmarks: U.S. v. Epic Games (order finalised March 2023, $245m refunds; bars charging via dark patterns and bars locking accounts over disputed charges) and U.S. v. Cognosphere LLC (complaint filed 17 January 2025, C.D. Cal., $20m; bars loot-box sales to under-16s without parental consent and targets confusing multi-step currency conversion). CORRECTED (audit defect 6): Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y.), Judge Denise Cote, is NOT an FTC Act § 5 or COPPA case — FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action and the FTC was not a party. It was a competitor suit under the LANHAM ACT and NEW YORK GENERAL BUSINESS LAW. An April 2026 jury returned a $420m verdict; the 28 July 2026 judgment separately awarded $719m in disgorgement as an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may ELECT IN LIEU OF damages, plus $10.1m in fees — alternative, not cumulative, so '$719m plus $10.1m' as a running total is wrong. It is a district-court judgment, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, not final, and NOT PRECEDENT anywhere (audit addition, missing item 3). The operational lesson survives all of that: FACT//DUEL's duel mode must never pit a paying player against an AI without unmissable disclosure, and a competitor can bring this claim with no regulator involved at all.

checklist.item: ROSCA-compliant subscription flow: clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms before billing information is taken, express informed consent, and a simple cancellation mechanism through the same medium used to subscribe
checklist.issuer: Federal Trade Commission
checklist.appliesTo: D; also A if coin packs auto-renew
checklist.prerequisite: Subscription UX and billing integration
checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. §§ 8403-8404. CORRECTED (audit defect 4): the FTC's 2024 AMENDED Negative Option Rule (the click-to-cancel regime) was vacated in its entirety by the Eighth Circuit in Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC, No. 24-3137 (8th Cir. 8 July 2025). That vacatur restored the pre-existing 1973 PRENOTIFICATION NEGATIVE OPTION RULE, which REMAINS IN FORCE at 16 C.F.R. Part 425 (audit addition, missing item 4). It is wrong to say 'there is currently no FTC negative option rule' — there is currently no CLICK-TO-CANCEL rule. Check whether your offer is a prenotification plan within Part 425. The FTC restarted the rulemaking: draft ANPRM submitted to OIRA 30 January 2026, ANPRM PUBLISHED 11 MARCH 2026, comments due 13 April 2026; it asks both whether to amend the EXISTING rule and about certain provisions of the vacated click-to-cancel rule. ROSCA and § 5 enforcement continues throughout. Build to click-to-cancel standards regardless — and note that in several states it is not optional (see the state automatic-renewal item below).

checklist.item: AUDIT ADDITION — State automatic-renewal law (ARL) compliance for any subscription: state-specific pre-consent disclosure, affirmative consent capture, acknowledgement/retention of terms, online cancellation mechanism, and renewal reminder notices
checklist.issuer: State attorneys general and private plaintiffs under state automatic-renewal statutes (California ARL, New York, and others)
checklist.appliesTo: D primarily; A if coin packs auto-renew
checklist.prerequisite: Subscription UX; state launch list
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION (missing item 6). The original brief verdicted Model D 'lawful' on the federal layer and told the founder to build to click-to-cancel standards 'anyway' for prudential reasons. That understates the position: several states impose click-to-cancel-equivalent obligations as BINDING LAW independent of any FTC rule, and they survived the Eighth Circuit vacatur untouched. California's Automatic Renewal Law and New York's automatic-renewal provisions are the usual leads; specific code sections, thresholds, reminder-notice intervals and effective dates are UNVERIFIED in this federal lane. Route to the state lane or to counsel before launching any subscription. Treat this as a compliance requirement, not prudence.

checklist.item: AUDIT ADDITION — State money transmitter licensing programme: 50-state analysis, licence applications, surety bonds, minimum net worth, permissible-investment rules, control-person background checks, NMLS filings and ongoing reporting
checklist.issuer: State banking / financial institutions regulators via NMLS (Nationwide Multistate Licensing System)
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory; C if you hold withdrawable user balances or the pool is entrant-funded
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED — bonding and net-worth minimums vary by state; the brief's own narrative calls this 'a multi-year, multi-million-dollar programme'
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — measured in quarters to years per state, not weeks
checklist.prerequisite: FinCEN Form 107 registration; audited financials; entity and control-person disclosures; written legal opinion on the model
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION (missing item 8). The original brief discussed this only in the risks narrative, never as a checklist action, even while calling it 'the real cost driver for Models B and C'. FinCEN Form 107 is a federal REGISTRATION with no approval step and authorises money transmission in NO state. Roughly every state requires its own money transmitter licence. This is outside the federal lane for substance but belongs on the action list because a founder working the checklist top-to-bottom would otherwise never see it — and because it, not federal law, is what determines whether Models B and C are financeable at all. All state-specific figures UNVERIFIED here.

checklist.item: Payment processor / acquirer onboarding for a gaming merchant: Reg GG representations, correct merchant category coding, and a written legal opinion on the model
checklist.issuer: Acquiring bank / card networks (obligations flow from the Federal Reserve Board and U.S. Treasury joint rule)
checklist.appliesTo: B, C; A and D onboard as ordinary digital-goods merchants
checklist.prerequisite: Entity, model description, counsel opinion, geolocation and age-verification stack
checklist.notes: Regulation GG, 12 C.F.R. Part 233 (Federal Reserve) / 31 C.F.R. Part 132 (Treasury), implementing 31 U.S.C. §§ 5361-5367; final rule published 73 Fed. Reg. 69382 (18 November 2008), effective 19 January 2009, compliance date extended to 1 June 2010. It obliges participants in the five designated payment systems (ACH, card systems, check collection, money transmitting businesses, wire transfer) to maintain policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent restricted transactions. In practice this is the real-world gate: your acquirer, not the DOJ, is what stops Model B or C from going live.

checklist.item: Geolocation and identity/age verification stack, with a state-by-state allow/deny list enforced at deposit and at stake time
checklist.issuer: Commercial vendors; no federal registration
checklist.prerequisite: State-by-state legal analysis (outside this federal lane)
checklist.notes: No federal statute mandates this directly, but 31 U.S.C. § 5362(10)(B)(i)(II) treats age and location verification as a defining feature of a lawful intrastate transaction, acquirers require it under Reg GG, and it is the only mechanism that keeps you out of § 5363 and § 1955 exposure in states that ban your model. Building money play without it is not a shortcut — it is the defect. Sequence the deny list from the subdivisions rows below, all of which are secondary-sourced and must be confirmed against primary statutes.

checklist.item: App store real-money gaming approval
checklist.issuer: Apple (App Review Guidelines) and Google (Google Play Real-Money Gambling, Games, and Contests policy)
checklist.appliesTo: B, C; A and D are ordinary IAP
checklist.prerequisite: Licence/registration evidence, geo-restriction, age gating
checklist.notes: Platform policy, NOT law — but it is a hard commercial gate that stops more products than federal law does. Apple's gaming/gambling provisions sit at App Review Guidelines § 5.3; verify the current numbering and the current Google Play policy text directly before relying on either. UNVERIFIED as of this correction pass.

checklist.item: Written US regulatory opinion from gaming counsel covering the federal analysis AND every launch state, refreshed at least annually
checklist.issuer: External US gaming/regulatory counsel
checklist.appliesTo: B, C mandatory; A and D advisable before any coin economics change
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec: coin flows, prize funding, matchmaking, withdrawal mechanics
checklist.notes: This checklist is compliance research, not legal advice. The federal layer is the easy half; the state layer decides whether you can operate, and it moved substantially in 2025-2026. Brief counsel specifically on: (a) Rev. Rul. 57-521 versus AM 2020-009 for the excise-tax position; (b) 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) — not FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 — for a dollar-denominated balance; (c) Marchetti/Grosso before any Form 11-C filing at the unauthorised rate; (d) the § 5363 'engaged in the business of betting or wagering' threshold and the § 1084(b) safe harbour.

checklist.item: Geofence the hard-prohibition states before ANY real-money feature ships: AZ, AR, CT, DE, FL, LA, MT, NV, SC, SD, TN, WA (12). Server-side, on deposit AND on contest entry, with VPN/proxy detection and a device-level check — not client-side IP alone.
checklist.issuer: Self-executing state criminal statutes; enforced by state AGs and gaming regulators
checklist.cost: Engineering + geolocation vendor fee (UNVERIFIED — gaming-grade geolocation vendors do not publish rates). Note the vendor itself takes on liability in CA, NY and OK, which is a pricing and willingness-to-onboard factor.
checklist.leadTime: Must be live before the first paid transaction
checklist.prerequisite: Server-authoritative accounts with a verified state of residence; FACT//DUEL is currently local-only IndexedDB with no accounts, so accounts are a hard prerequisite
checklist.notes: This is the industry-standard block list. Skillz's published legal terms restrict real-prize play in AZ, AR, CT, DE, LA, MT, SC, SD, TN (9) and additionally ME and IN where playing cards are involved. Add NV (licence state, no commercially viable licence), FL (Fla. Stat. s.849.14) and WA (RCW 9.46.240, Class C felony) for a defensible 12. CORRECTED: MONTANA STAYS ON THIS LIST but for a different reason than the brief gave. Montana is NOT a skill-wagering-statute state — Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 is 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' and defines nothing (verified at mca.legmt.gov, 14 Sep 2026), and s.23-5-112 contains no 'contest of skill' definition; Montana's gambling definition at s.23-5-112(14)(a) is chance-based. Montana is on the list because of S.B. 555 (dual-currency ban, eff. 1 Oct 2025). For Model C specifically, Montana is now UNRESOLVED rather than absolutely barred and a Montana opinion could remove it. [AUDIT ADDITION] Geofencing protects the OPERATOR from the operator-side offence. It does not by itself resolve PLAYER-SIDE liability under statutes that reach the person who plays (720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1); Cal. Penal Code s.337a reaches accepting AND making a bet) — build the terms of service and the refund/return-of-balance posture on that assumption.

checklist.item: Geofence or disable dual-currency redemption in the states with 2025-26 online-sweepstakes legislation. CORRECTED: this is TEN states with an EXPRESS DUAL-CURRENCY PROHIBITION (CA, CT, IN, LA, ME, MT, NJ, NY, OK, TN) plus TWO with an OPEN-ENDED ENFORCEMENT-AUTHORITY GRANT and no statutory dual-currency definition (IA, NV). The brief counted all twelve as bans; they are not the same compliance question. Several also make YOUR VENDORS liable.
checklist.issuer: CA AG/DOJ; CT DCP; IN Gaming Commission; IA Racing & Gaming Commission; LA Gaming Control Board; ME Gambling Control Unit; MT Dept of Justice Gambling Control; NV Gaming Control Board; NJ DGE; NY Gaming Commission and AG; OK; TN AG
checklist.cost: Statutory penalties if breached: CA $1,000-$25,000/violation plus up to 1 yr (confirmed); NY $10,000-$100,000/violation (confirmed); OK Class C2 felony (confirmed); CT Class D felony; NJ $100,000 first offence / $250,000 subsequent (text confirmed, enactment UNVERIFIED); IN civil to $100,000 (UNVERIFIED); LA to $100,000 plus racketeering (UNVERIFIED).
checklist.leadTime: In force as at 14 Sep 2026 for every one of these except Oklahoma. [AUDIT ADDITION] EFFECTIVE-DATE SEQUENCING: OKLAHOMA S.B. 1589 takes effect 1 NOV 2026 and is the ONLY listed prohibition not yet operative today. Dates: NY 5 Dec 2025 (confirmed); CA 1 Jan 2026 (confirmed); CT and MT 1 Oct 2025; OK 1 Nov 2026 (confirmed, veto overridden 14 May 2026). NJ '15 Aug 2025', IN and IA '1 Jul 2026', ME 'Jul 2026', TN '22 May 2026' and LA '1 Aug 2026' are all UNVERIFIED signing/effect dates — [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] keep them as working assumptions only and confirm from the enrolled bills before they enter a launch plan. Do NOT stage the geofence to launch into Oklahoma before 1 Nov 2026: the window is seven weeks, the conduct is a Class C2 felony from day one after, and there is no wind-down provision.
checklist.prerequisite: Legal determination of whether FACT//DUEL 'simulates casino-style gambling' — most of the ten express bans require that element and a trivia duel arguably does not, but CA Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) and FL s.849.14 catch skill wagering independently. In IOWA and NEVADA there is no such definitional element to argue against: the question is whether the Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission or the Nevada Gaming Control Board decides to act, which cannot be resolved by reading the statute and is therefore HARDER, not easier, to plan around.
checklist.notes: CA Penal Code s.337o, NY Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912 and OK S.B. 1589 all extend liability to payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, content suppliers and MEDIA AFFILIATES who knowingly support the platform. That means your Stripe/Adyen equivalent, your geolocation vendor and your affiliate marketers can be prosecuted — in practice they will refuse to onboard you.

checklist.item: Decide whether you will HOLD player funds at all — and then answer the THRESHOLD question the brief skipped: are you transmitting money TO ANOTHER PERSON? CORRECTED: state money transmitter licensing is not an automatic consequence of holding player funds.
checklist.issuer: State banking/financial-institution departments, applied for through NMLS (Nationwide Multistate Licensing System)
checklist.appliesTo: B (squarely). C only if a transmission-to-another-person analysis says so — do not assume it.
checklist.cost: IF required: application fees commonly $500-$10,000 per state plus investigation, fingerprint and NMLS processing fees; surety bonds from $10,000 (WA, WY) to $500,000 (NY), California scaling to $7,000,000 on volume; tangible net worth the greater of $100,000 or 3% of total assets up to $100m under the MTMA formula. All figures are aggregated from licensing-consultancy and law-firm sources, NOT from state fee schedules — re-price from current NMLS state-specific requirements before budgeting.
checklist.leadTime: 3-12 months per state for a complete application; New York and California commonly 12-18 months or longer
checklist.prerequisite: Audited financials, business plan, BSA/AML programme, background checks on control persons, FinCEN MSB registration (federal — out of this lane)
checklist.notes: CORRECTED, and this matters more than any other line in the checklist. Most state MTL regimes — and the CSBS MTMA definition this brief relies on elsewhere — turn on RECEIVING MONEY FOR TRANSMISSION TO ANOTHER PERSON. An operator that takes deposits and pays its OWN prize obligations out of its OWN funds is frequently not transmitting to a third party and may fall outside the definition entirely in many states. That is precisely MODEL C: operator-funded, fixed, entrant-count-independent prizes. MODEL B — where you hold one player's stake for payment to another player — squarely raises money transmission. The brief's flat '49 states plus DC, the single largest cost and time line item in the whole plan' materially OVERSTATES the burden for the very design it recommends. Correct posture: assume a full 49-state-plus-DC programme for Model B (multi-year, seven-figure, effectively disqualifying for a startup); for Model C, get a money-transmission opinion on the transmission-to-another-person question FIRST, because the answer may be that no licence is required at all. Which states depart from the transmission-to-another-person formulation is UNVERIFIED and is the specific question to put to counsel.

checklist.item: AVOID the MTL problem structurally: never take custody of player funds. Route deposits and payouts through a licensed payment provider or sponsor bank so that the provider, not you, is the money transmitter.
checklist.issuer: Commercial (licensed PSP / bank partner)
checklist.prerequisite: Contract that makes the PSP the holder of record; you must not have the ability to direct player funds
checklist.notes: 42 states recognise an agent-of-payee exemption (via MTMA adoption or their own pre-existing law). Eight do NOT have an explicit agent-of-payee exemption: FL, NJ, NM, OK, OR, RI, UT, WY (secondary source — Finextra/Cornerstone Licensing, 2026; verify with counsel before relying).

checklist.item: Understand that the Money Transmission Modernization Act does NOT give you one licence. CORRECTED: the brief's '31 states have enacted the MTMA ... Massachusetts became the 26th adopter' is internally inconsistent — 31 enacted and Massachusetts as the 26th cannot both be right in the same sentence. TREAT THE ADOPTER COUNT AS UNVERIFIED.
checklist.issuer: Conference of State Bank Supervisors (model law); adopted state by state
checklist.cost: n/a — it harmonises net worth, surety bond and permissible-investment standards, not fees
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: The operative conclusion does not depend on the count and should be stated without false precision: PLAN FOR 49 APPLICATIONS, NOT ONE. CSBS says MTMA states cover the large majority of reported money transmission activity, but Cooley is explicit that 'managing compliance with money transmission laws generally remains a state-by-state proposition' — states added bespoke provisions, excluded payroll processors, and diverged on bonds (Maine set a fixed bond instead of the model formula). Massachusetts (eff. 1 Jan 2026) and Virginia (eff. 1 Jul 2026) are reported adopters; the roster and the total are UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: Restructure the paid product to Model C: fixed prize pool, announced BEFORE entries open, funded by the operator, NOT scaled to entrant count, with the operator as a neutral non-participant taking no rake from a player-funded pot.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.cost: Operator-funded prize liability (a real P&L cost, unlike a rake)
checklist.prerequisite: Kill player-v-player escrow entirely on the paid path
checklist.notes: This tracks the design attributes the New York Court of Appeals treated as characteristic of lawful skill competition in White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (2022): 'skill-based competitions in which participants who exercise substantial influence over the outcome of the contest are awarded predetermined fixed prizes by a neutral operator'. CORRECTED — DO NOT TREAT THIS AS CLEARANCE. White v. Cuomo was decided under Article I s.9 of the NEW YORK CONSTITUTION, about interactive fantasy sports that the legislature had affirmatively authorized in Racing Law article 14 AND expressly exempted from Penal Law article 225. It has no precedential force outside New York, and it does NOT hold that an unauthorized paid-entry trivia contest escapes the material-degree contest-of-chance test at N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1). The brief's instruction to 'build to that sentence' would let a founder conclude New York is cleared by design compliance alone. It is not. Use the three attributes as a design target; get a New York opinion separately. The reported 4-3 vote split is UNVERIFIED — do not cite it. An entrant-count-dependent pot converts the structure back into a wager and loses even the design argument.

checklist.item: Remove every chance element from the paid path: no randomised question draw, no randomised opponent variance affecting payout, no loot-box or gacha reveal, no variable multiplier. Same question set, same order, same conditions for all entrants in a contest.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.prerequisite: Separate paid contest engine from the free duel engine
checklist.notes: This is what defeats the material-element states (N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1) 'Contest of chance' — CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(2), which is 'Gambling'; also AL, KY, MO, OH, OR, WA) and Tennessee's near-any-chance test (Tenn. Code s.39-17-501(1), 'to any degree contingent on chance'). FACT//DUEL's Expedition mechanic — staking points at three confidence tiers on rotating question sets — is the highest-risk surface here and must not carry real money.

checklist.item: Keep purchased coins structurally incapable of being staked. If a user buys coins, those coins must only ever be spent at a fixed price on a fixed item.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.prerequisite: Two separate ledgers: purchased (spend-only) and earned (stakeable, worthless)
checklist.notes: Directly addresses Kater v. Churchill Downs, 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 2018) and RCW 9.46.0285, and the identical New York wording at Penal Law s.225.00(6) ('Something of value') — CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(1), which is 'Contest of chance'. Subdivision verified at nysenate.gov, 14 Sep 2026. A credit that extends the privilege of playing IS a thing of value; a staked-and-lost purchased coin is gambling in Washington with no cash-out at all.

checklist.item: New York games-of-chance registration and bond if any promotion's total announced prize value exceeds $5,000.
checklist.issuer: New York Department of State
checklist.cost: $100 non-refundable filing fee plus a surety bond or certificate of deposit equal to the total prize value
checklist.leadTime: File at least 30 days before the start date
checklist.prerequisite: Final rules and prize schedule
checklist.notes: N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law art. 24-A s.369-e. Secondary sources: Klein Moynihan Turco and Fasthoff Law Firm compliance guides. Applies to games of CHANCE — a properly structured skill contest may fall outside it, which is itself a reason to document the skill analysis.

checklist.item: Florida game promotion filing and trust account or bond if total prize value exceeds $5,000.
checklist.issuer: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS)
checklist.cost: Trust account or surety bond for the total prize value; filing fee UNVERIFIED
checklist.leadTime: File rules and prize list at least 7 days before the promotion
checklist.prerequisite: Final rules
checklist.notes: Fla. Stat. s.849.094. NOTE: this does not cure Fla. Stat. s.849.14, which independently makes it unlawful to bet on the result of a contest of skill. Florida should be geofenced for paid play regardless; s.849.094 matters only for free-entry promotions.

checklist.item: Rhode Island promotion registration where total announced prize value exceeds $500 (retail-linked promotions). [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] Hawaii registration and bond for entry-fee contests with prizes of $5,000 or more — THE AUDIT RECOMMENDS STRIKING THE HAWAII LINE ENTIRELY; it is retained here only as a contested item.
checklist.issuer: Rhode Island Secretary of State; Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
checklist.cost: RI: no surety bond required (secondary source). HI: UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Final rules
checklist.notes: Both thresholds come from promotions-law compliance guides (Sweeppea, Fasthoff, Klein Moynihan Turco), not from a primary statute. [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] ON HAWAII SPECIFICALLY: no Hawaii prize-promotion registration statute could be identified, and the claim sits badly next to the brief's own correct observation that Hawaii permits no legal gambling of any kind and has NO GAMING REGULATOR — there is no agency to register with. The operational danger is that a founder reads this line as meaning paid entry in Hawaii is curable by filing. IT IS NOT. GEOFENCE HAWAII. Do not attempt a Hawaii registration route without a primary cite from counsel. Verify the RI cite before relying on it too.

checklist.item: Do NOT rely on Arizona's amusement-gambling intellectual-contest registration as a route into Arizona.
checklist.issuer: Arizona Attorney General
checklist.leadTime: Register before conducting the event; file winners' names and addresses within 10 days of awarding prizes
checklist.prerequisite: A sworn statement that no increment was added to an established purchase price
checklist.notes: A.R.S. s.13-3311 exists and is a real registration regime for intellectual contests — but the underlying A.R.S. s.13-3301(4) exception it supports caps prizes at merchandise worth under $10 wholesale (coupon aggregate $550) and requires that the payment be part of an established purchase price with no increment. A cash-prize trivia contest cannot fit. Arizona is a geofence, not a registration.

checklist.item: Adopt an age gate — CORRECTED: not a flat 18+. Age of majority is 19 in Alabama and Nebraska and 21 in Mississippi, so use 18+ generally, 19+ in AL and NE, 21+ in MS, and 21+ in any state where the product could be characterised as gambling — with real identity verification on the paid path, not a self-declared date of birth.
checklist.issuer: State AGs (UDAP), plus app store policy
checklist.prerequisite: Accounts and server-side identity
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION] The brief prescribed a flat 18+ gate. Below the age of majority a minor can generally disaffirm the contract, which affects (a) enforceability of the terms of service and of the ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND CLASS-ACTION WAIVER the brief elsewhere tells the founder to build — the waiver is worth little against a user who can void the agreement — and (b) the minors' in-app-purchase exposure the brief correctly identifies as the most common consumer-protection enforcement hook against games. Current statutory cites for the AL/NE/MS majority ages are UNVERIFIED; confirm with counsel. Also a prerequisite for any MTL/BSA programme and for New Jersey's esports rule (participants 18+).

checklist.item: Automatic-renewal compliance for the subscription product: express affirmative consent, free-trial/free-to-pay-conversion disclosure, 7-30 day advance notice of fee changes, and same-medium (in-app) cancellation.
checklist.issuer: California AG and district attorneys; Virginia AG; New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
checklist.leadTime: CA in force since 1 Jul 2025; VA 1 Jul 2026; NYC 1 Oct 2026
checklist.prerequisite: In-app cancel flow
checklist.notes: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code s.17600 et seq. as amended by A.B. 2863 (signed 24 Sep 2024). About 25 states have automatic-renewal laws; California, Virginia and NYC are the strictest. Selling via Apple/Google billing satisfies much of the cancellation mechanics but not the disclosure obligations.

checklist.item: Build the arbitration clause, class-action waiver and loss-recovery mitigation strategy BEFORE launch, because state gambling-loss-recovery statutes are the main private-litigation threat and they do not require a criminal conviction.
checklist.issuer: Private plaintiffs' bar (and, in Kentucky, 'any other person' after six months under KRS 372.040)
checklist.cost: Exposure is uncapped: Big Fish Casino settled Kater-line claims for $155m (secondary source, widely reported)
checklist.prerequisite: Terms of service and dispute-resolution design
checklist.notes: Verified live statutes: Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (recover losses of $50+ from the winner); Washington RCW 4.24.070. KENTUCKY — CORRECTED: the brief packed two sections into one number. KRS 372.020 is the LOSER'S OWN action to recover the amount lost ($5 or more). KRS 372.040 is the separate provision carrying the six-month window, the 'any other person' standing and TREBLE damages. Splitting them matters because s.372.040 is the provision that creates the outsized exposure. Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and Ohio have analogous statutes and were used in the 2026 prediction-market class actions against Kalshi, Robinhood and Webull (secondary: Illinois Answers Project, Mar 2026). [AUDIT ADDITION] Note the interaction with the age-gate item: an arbitration clause and class waiver do not reliably bind a user below the age of majority (19 in AL and NE, 21 in MS).

checklist.item: Confirm Apple App Store and Google Play real-money policy clearance before building the payment surface.
checklist.issuer: Apple; Google
checklist.cost: Store commission on any in-app purchase; nil for external real-money wallets where permitted
checklist.prerequisite: Evidence of licensure or a legal opinion, plus geo-restriction to permitted territories
checklist.notes: Both stores require real-money gaming apps to be geo-restricted to jurisdictions where the developer is licensed and to be submitted by the licensed entity. CORRECTED: the brief said 'no state licence exists for peer-to-peer trivia wagering'. Licences do exist in principle — Nevada NRS 463.160 licenses any game played for money with no skill/chance distinction, and New Jersey's DGE licenses esports event wagering — but none is available to this product at viable cost or lead time, so the practical conclusion is unchanged: MODEL B IS VERY LIKELY UNSHIPPABLE ON BOTH STORES. Policy citation UNVERIFIED — read the current guidelines directly before commissioning legal opinions.

checklist.item: Commission a per-state legal opinion from gaming counsel covering all 51 jurisdictions before the first real-money launch, and a separate money-transmission opinion.
checklist.issuer: Private gaming counsel
checklist.cost: One published market data point: $15,000 for a 51-jurisdiction skill-gaming opinion (terms.law/Tokmakov advertised price). Full-service gaming firms will be materially more.
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec — counsel cannot opine on a moving design
checklist.notes: Walters Law Group's published position is that 'the only reliable way to evaluate the legality of a particular skill game in the United States is to engage experienced gaming counsel to render a legal opinion' and that any blanket list of legal states is unreliable. One firm reported reaching ZERO unconditionally cleared states in a recent comprehensive engagement. Treat this checklist as a map, not an opinion. [AUDIT ADDITION] The opinion scope must now also cover: (a) tribal compact exclusivity in CA, FL, OK and CT; (b) the money-transmission threshold question (transmission to another person) rather than assuming a 49-state programme; (c) player-side as distinct from operator-side liability; (d) unclaimed-property duties on unredeemed coin balances; and (e) whether an AMOE / free-entry structure opens any state that paid entry closes.

checklist.item: Maintain a legislative watch list — this area changed materially three times in 18 months and will change again.
checklist.issuer: n/a
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: Live pending: DC B26-0656 (Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, would ban sweepstakes while legalising iGaming); Ohio HB 298; Virginia SB 579; Maryland HB 1226/HB 295/SB 652; Missouri HB 1251. Failed in 2026 but likely to return: Minnesota SF 4474/HF 4410; Florida SB 1580/HB 1467; Massachusetts H 4431; Mississippi SB 2104; Hawaii SB 3281; Texas SB 517; Arkansas SB 524. Active enforcement without legislation: Illinois Gaming Board issued 60+ cease-and-desist letters on 3 Mar 2026; Mississippi Gaming Commission C&Ds; New York AG Letitia James C&Ds to 26 platforms in Mar 2025; Kentucky AG litigation against VGW; Pennsylvania Supreme Court held in June 2026 that 'skill games' are slot machines under PA law.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Obtain a tribal-gaming exposure assessment before any real-money launch, separately from the criminal-code analysis.
checklist.issuer: Tribal gaming authorities and their counsel; state-tribal compact administrators (CA, FL, OK, CT among others)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — run in parallel with the gaming-counsel opinion, not after it
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec
checklist.notes: The original brief never mentioned tribal gaming. Exclusivity provisions in state-tribal compacts in California, Florida, Oklahoma and Connecticut give tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming, and tribal objection has killed products that had a clean reading of the state criminal code. Oklahoma additionally grants tribal operators exclusive online gambling rights. This risk sits ALONGSIDE the statutes analysed in this lane, not inside them: clearing the penal code does not clear a compact objection. Specific compact provisions and their reach to a non-casino skill product are UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Build an unclaimed-property / escheat programme for unredeemed coin and credit balances.
checklist.issuer: State treasurers / unclaimed property administrators (all 51 jurisdictions)
checklist.appliesTo: A, D (and B, C wherever a balance can sit dormant)
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED — reporting and remittance of the balance itself plus administration
checklist.leadTime: Annual reporting cycles; dormancy periods commonly measured in years, so this bites after launch, not before
checklist.prerequisite: Server-authoritative per-user balance ledger with last-activity timestamps — FACT//DUEL's current local-only IndexedDB store cannot support this
checklist.notes: The original brief cleared Models A and D as 'lawful' with no caveat beyond in-app-purchase disclosure. Both accumulate STORED VALUE. Several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as abandoned property with reporting and remittance duties to the state. Whether closed-loop, non-redeemable game currency is exempt varies by state and is the specific question to ask. Thresholds, dormancy periods and exemptions per state: UNVERIFIED. The design consequence is concrete: build last-activity tracking and a balance-expiry/notice policy now rather than retrofitting it.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Decide and document the PLAYER-SIDE liability posture, separately from the operator-side geofence.
checklist.issuer: n/a — terms of service and product policy
checklist.prerequisite: The per-state opinion must be scoped to answer it
checklist.notes: The brief disentangled player-side from operator-side liability only for Illinois. Several of the statutes it relies on reach the PERSON WHO PLAYS OR BETS, not just the house: 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('plays a game of chance or skill for money'), and Cal. Penal Code s.337a, which reaches making and ACCEPTING a bet. Illinois has a participant-side bona fide contest exception that does NOT shelter the operator; the mirror-image question — whether the operator's geofence leaves an individual user exposed — has to be answered too, because it drives the terms of service, the refund posture, and whether a balance must be returned to a user who played from a prohibited state. Per-state scope of player-side liability: UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Cost the free-entry / alternative-method-of-entry (AMOE) option before committing to Model C, and understand that it is the most legislatively targeted structure in the country right now.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control, with counsel
checklist.cost: Engineering plus fulfilment of free entries; prize liability unchanged
checklist.prerequisite: A per-state opinion on whether removing consideration actually opens any state you care about
checklist.notes: The brief jumped from Model B to Model C without evaluating a genuine AMOE. A free entry of equal dignity (no purchase necessary, equal odds, equal prize eligibility, a real and usable free path) removes the CONSIDERATION element and can open states whose bar is consideration-based. It does NOT help where the statute does not turn on consideration in that way — Arizona, Florida, Delaware, South Dakota and Louisiana among them. And the decisive caution: THE ENTIRE 2025-26 DUAL-CURRENCY BAN WAVE CATALOGUED IN THIS LANE IS THE LEGISLATIVE RESPONSE TO EXACTLY THIS STRUCTURE — sweepstakes operators used an AMOE to argue they were not gambling, and ten states legislated against it. An AMOE is a legitimate option for a promotional contest; it is not a safe harbour in 2026. Which states it opens: UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Sequence the geofence against effective dates, and treat Oklahoma (1 Nov 2026) as the only prohibition on this list not yet operative as at today, 14 Sep 2026.
checklist.issuer: n/a — launch planning
checklist.prerequisite: Geofence implemented as a configuration table with per-state effective dates, not hard-coded logic
checklist.notes: The brief listed in-force dates from 5 Dec 2025 to 1 Nov 2026 but never told a founder what to do about the gap. As at 14 Sep 2026: NY (5 Dec 2025), CT and MT (1 Oct 2025), CA (1 Jan 2026) are in force; the IN, IA, ME, TN and LA dates are UNVERIFIED but all fall before today if correct; OKLAHOMA S.B. 1589 is the single listed prohibition still to come, effective 1 NOV 2026. DO NOT STAGE A LAUNCH INTO OKLAHOMA IN THE SEVEN-WEEK WINDOW. The conduct becomes a Class C2 felony with no wind-down, the definitions are the broadest of the 2026 wave, liability extends to your payment and geolocation vendors, and Oklahoma also has tribal exclusivity over online gambling. Ship the geofence with Oklahoma already blocked and a per-state effective-date column so the next wave is a config change.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Re-verify, from the enrolled bills, the five 2026 enactments whose dates this lane could not confirm: Indiana H.B. 1052 / P.L. 153-2026; Iowa S.F. 2289; Maine L.D. 2007; Tennessee S.B. 2136; New Jersey A5447.
checklist.issuer: n/a — verification task
checklist.leadTime: Before any date from this lane enters a launch timeline
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] This is a verification flag, not an allegation of fabrication. Every 2025-26 enactment that COULD be reached checked out exactly: CA AB 831 (signed 11 Oct 2025, Ch. 623, adds Penal Code s.337o); NY S5935A (signed 5 Dec 2025, Ch. 605, adds Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912, $10,000-$100,000 per violation); OK S.B. 1589 (vetoed 7 May 2026, overridden 14 May 2026, Class C2 felony, eff. 1 Nov 2026, with the dual-currency 'representative of value' definition and geolocation/platform/media-affiliate liability verbatim as described). For the other five, primary legislative sources were blocked, JS-rendered or empty. NJ A5447's TEXT is confirmed to exist and to target dual-currency sweepstakes with civil penalties of $100,000 first / $250,000 subsequent, but its ENACTMENT and the 15 Aug 2025 signing date are not confirmed. Confirm all five before relying on the specific dates.

risks: STATE-LAW PREEMPTION REALITY — THERE IS NONE. 31 U.S.C. § 5361(b) is an express rule of construction: 'No provision of this subchapter shall be construed as altering, limiting, or extending any Federal or State law or Tribal-State compact prohibiting, permitting, or regulating gambling' in the United States. PASPA was struck down in Murphy v. NCAA (2018), removing the only modern federal attempt to constrain state choice. UIGEA (§ 5362(10)(A)), the Illegal Gambling Business Act (18 U.S.C. § 1955(b)(1)(i)) and the Travel Act (18 U.S.C. § 1952) all take their unlawfulness FROM state law. Clearing the federal layer tells you almost nothing about whether you can operate in any given state.

THE UIGEA 'EDUCATIONAL GAME OR CONTEST' TRAP. § 5362(1)(E)(ix) reads 'participation in any fantasy or simulation sports game or educational game or contest...' and is routinely quoted as if those opening words were a self-contained carve-out for quiz products. They are not. Clause (ix) imposes three cumulative conditions, and (ix)(II) requires outcomes 'determined predominantly by accumulated statistical results of the performance of individuals ... in multiple real-world sporting or other events'. No trivia game can satisfy that. If any adviser tells the founder that FACT//DUEL is a UIGEA-exempt 'educational contest', that adviser has misread the statute.

CORRECTED RISK — THE FEDERAL WAGERING EXCISE TAX IS A MODEL B PROBLEM, NOT A MODEL C KILLER. The original brief said this was 'the most likely way this product loses money quietly', that § 4421 'makes no skill/chance distinction', and that AM 2020-009 applied §§ 4401/4411 to DFS 'on exactly that basis'. The audit refuted all three at 'certain' confidence and this pass adopts the refutation. AM 2020-009 states the statute 'does not differentiate whether an activity involves skill, chance, or some combination of the two' and then immediately says 'Still, the presence or absence of skill in a contest may help determine whether an entry fee constitutes a taxable wager, or not', distinguishing DFS from Rev. Rul. 57-521's puzzle contest on the ground that the DFS entrant 'has no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players'. Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 holds that an entry fee in a contest of mental skill with a guaranteed operator-funded prize is not a wager 'unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'. WHAT REMAINS TRUE: the 2% unauthorised rate is levied on HANDLE, not net revenue, so IF the analysis goes against you the tax can exceed gross margin — model it. But for Model C with an operator-funded fixed prize the leading authority is favourable, and for Model B (stake money alone comprising the prize) it is adverse. The risk is Model B's, and the residual Model C risk is that chance elements — question draw, matchmaking, reaction-time scoring — pull the product toward the DFS side of the line the IRS itself drew.

AUDIT ADDITION — DO NOT FILE FORM 11-C WITHOUT A FIFTH AMENDMENT ANALYSIS. The checklist tells the founder to register before accepting any wagers, and the $500 rate applies where wagers are NOT authorised under the law of the state where accepted. Filing at that rate is a signed, dated federal admission of accepting unauthorised wagers — i.e. potential evidence in a 18 U.S.C. § 1955 or state gambling prosecution. Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968) and Grosso v. United States held the self-incrimination privilege a complete defence to failure-to-register/pay prosecutions under the then-existing wagering tax scheme. The CURRENT scope of the privilege after later amendments to §§ 4411/4412 is UNVERIFIED here. Settle it with counsel before filing. A compliance step that manufactures the evidence for a criminal case is not a compliance step.

MODEL A DEGRADES INTO MODEL B ON A SINGLE PRODUCT DECISION. One cash-out path, one peer-to-peer coin transfer, one 'redeem coins for a gift card' feature, or one tournament that pays a prize of value, and the coin becomes convertible virtual currency, FinCEN money-transmitter obligations attach, and the state sweepstakes bans engage. FinCEN 'interprets these exemptions strictly' (FIN-2019-G001 at 9). Put a hard architectural boundary — not a policy note — between the closed-loop coin and anything redeemable. Note also the corrected authority position: once coins are SOLD, § 5362(1)(E)(viii) stops protecting them, so Model A's only remaining federal argument is 'no prize of value' under § 5362(1)(A). That argument fails the instant anything of value is paid out.

THE WIRE ACT IS NARROW BUT NOT SETTLED NATIONWIDE. N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 20 Jan. 2021) limits 18 U.S.C. § 1084 to sporting events, and DOJ did not seek certiorari. But the 2018 OLC opinion reading § 1084 to cover all interstate wagering has never been formally withdrawn, and the First Circuit's holding binds only Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico. In the other circuits there is no controlling authority. AUDIT ADDITION: the § 1084(b) safe harbour (transmission of information for use in news reporting, and transmission between jurisdictions where the betting is legal) is a threshold defence the original analysis skipped. Treat the Wire Act as low-probability, high-severity tail risk rather than a resolved question.

CORRECTED — BOTS AND MATCHMAKING ARE A NINE-FIGURE PRIVATE-LITIGATION RISK, BROUGHT BY COMPETITORS, NOT REGULATORS, AND NOT YET FINAL. Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y., Cote, J.) produced a $420m April 2026 jury verdict; the 28 July 2026 judgment separately awarded $719m in DISGORGEMENT as an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may elect IN LIEU OF damages, plus $10.1m in fees. The figures are alternative, not cumulative — the original brief's headline '$719m' and checklist '$719m plus $10.1m' read as a running total and overstate the award. The claims were under the LANHAM ACT and NEW YORK GENERAL BUSINESS LAW, not FTC Act § 5 or COPPA; the FTC was not a party and FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action. It is a district-court judgment, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, NOT FINAL, and NOT PRECEDENT anywhere. What survives every one of those corrections: the conduct found — marketing real-money 'skill-based head-to-head' tournaments while secretly filling them with bots — is precisely FACT//DUEL's exposure. The product currently has no server and no real opponents; whatever fills a duel must be audited and disclosed before a single dollar is staked. A competitor can bring this claim with no regulator interest at all.

MSB REGISTRATION IS NOT A LICENCE AND WILL NOT SATISFY THE STATES. FinCEN Form 107 is a federal registration with no approval step. It does not authorise money transmission in any state. Roughly every state requires its own money transmitter licence with bonding and net-worth requirements — a multi-year, multi-million-dollar programme that is outside this federal lane but is the real cost driver for Models B and C. It is now a checklist item (audit addition), not merely a narrative aside.

HOLDING USER BALANCES IS THE SINGLE DESIGN CHOICE THAT MOST CHANGES THE LEGAL ANSWER. A withdrawable cash balance makes the operator look like a money transmitter under 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) — which is the correct provision for dollar-denominated value, not FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 — even where the game itself is defensible. One-way payouts (money in, contest entered, prize paid out directly to the winner's funding instrument, no stored redeemable value) preserve the 'integral to the sale of services' exemption at § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F). This is worth designing around from day one and is the highest-leverage single decision in the whole file.

COPPA IS ALREADY IN FULL FORCE, NOT PENDING. The amended Rule's compliance date passed on 22 April 2026. A trivia product with cartoon-adjacent presentation, no accounts and no age gate is a plausible FTC target on child-directedness alone, entirely independently of anything to do with money. The FTC's 25 February 2026 age-verification enforcement policy statement is confirmed to exist but its CONDITIONS ARE UNVERIFIED — a hard under-18 block depends on collecting exactly the data that statement addresses, so read it before designing the gate.

AUDIT ADDITION — MODEL D IS NOT A CONSUMER-PROTECTION FREE PASS. Two corrections compound here: the 1973 Prenotification Negative Option Rule survived the click-to-cancel vacatur and remains at 16 C.F.R. Part 425, and state automatic-renewal laws (California, New York and others) impose click-to-cancel-equivalent duties as binding law. 'Federally lawful' plus 'build to click-to-cancel standards anyway' understated both. Model D is the cheapest model to launch and the easiest one to get sued over for a bad cancellation flow.

FEDERAL CLEARANCE ON MODEL A OR D DOES NOT MAKE THE CURRENT PRODUCT FUTURE-PROOF. The existing FREE demo-coin game sits squarely inside 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(E)(viii)(II) — 'points or credits that the sponsor of the game or contest provides to participants free of charge and that can be used or redeemed only for participation in games or contests offered by the sponsor'. That exclusion is written around free credits and it stops applying the moment coins are sold for money. It therefore protects today's product and none of the four proposed models.

AUDIT ADDITION — § 5363 HAS A THRESHOLD THE ORIGINAL ANALYSIS ASSUMED AWAY. 31 U.S.C. § 5363 prohibits acceptance of payment by 'a person engaged in the business of betting or wagering' in connection with unlawful internet gambling. Whether FACT//DUEL is such a person is a contestable element, not a given, particularly for Model C. Do not concede it. Argue the threshold before arguing the exclusions.

THE SKILL ARGUMENT DOES NOT SAVE MODEL B. CORRECTED COUNT: TEN states, not eleven, legislate around the skill/chance question — Arizona (gambling includes contests 'of chance or skill'), California Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) (bets on contests of skill BETWEEN PERSONS), Florida s.849.14, Delaware 11 Del. C. s.1403, Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('game of chance or skill'), Louisiana R.S. 14:90 (no chance element at all), Nevada NRS 463.0152 (no skill/chance distinction), South Dakota SDCL s.22-25A-1 (contest or game, no chance element), South Carolina (Chimento), Arkansas s.5-66-104. MONTANA IS REMOVED: the brief's Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 'paid entry disqualifies a skill contest' claim is withdrawn — that section is 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' and defines nothing, and Montana's actual gambling definition at s.23-5-112(14)(a) is chance-based (both verified at mca.legmt.gov, 14 Sep 2026). Any pitch deck or investor memo that says 'trivia is skill so we are fine' is still wrong on the law in the remaining ten.

YOUR VENDORS GO DOWN WITH YOU. California Penal Code s.337o, New York Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912 and Oklahoma S.B. 1589 all extend criminal or civil liability to payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, content and technology suppliers, platform providers, promoters and MEDIA AFFILIATES who knowingly support a prohibited operator. The practical consequence is not that you get prosecuted first — it is that no reputable PSP, geolocation vendor or affiliate network will onboard you, and any that does will terminate on first notice, stranding player balances mid-contest.

PRIVATE LOSS-RECOVERY LITIGATION IS A BIGGER THREAT THAN PROSECUTION. Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (recover losses of $50+); KENTUCKY — CORRECTED — KRS 372.020 (the loser's own action, $5+) AND THE SEPARATE KRS 372.040 (after six months, ANY OTHER PERSON may sue for TREBLE the loss); Washington RCW 4.24.070; plus analogues in Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and Ohio. s.372.040 is the provision that creates the real exposure: it turns a private remedy into a bounty available to strangers and litigation funders. These need no conviction, no regulator and no intent — just a player who lost money on an unlicensed game. The Kater line settled for a reported $155m. The 2026 class actions against Kalshi, Robinhood and Webull used exactly this machinery across five states at once, funded by a litigation-finance firm. [AUDIT ADDITION] An arbitration clause and class-action waiver are the standard mitigation but do not reliably bind users below the age of majority — 19 in Alabama and Nebraska, 21 in Mississippi.

WASHINGTON AND NEW YORK REACH MODEL A. RCW 9.46.0285 and N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(6) ('Something of value' — CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(1), which is 'Contest of chance'; verified at nysenate.gov 14 Sep 2026) both define a thing of value to include the privilege of playing a game without charge. Kater v. Churchill Downs (9th Cir. 2018) applied that to virtual chips. FACT//DUEL's existing demo-coin escrow — coins staked into escrow, winner takes the escrow — is structurally the same mechanic. If those coins ever become purchasable, the product is arguably illegal gambling in Washington with no cash-out feature at all. The fix is architectural and must be designed in now: purchased coins must be spend-only and structurally incapable of being staked.

THE 2026 LEGISLATIVE WAVE IS NOT OVER. CORRECTED: about TEN states enacted express dual-currency prohibitions between June 2025 and November 2026 (CA, CT, IN, LA, ME, MT, NJ, NY, OK, TN), and TWO more (IA, NV) granted regulators open-ended enforcement authority without defining the offence. Bills failed but will return in Minnesota, Florida, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Hawaii, Texas and Arkansas; bills are live in DC, Ohio, Virginia, Maryland and Missouri. A compliance posture built on today's map will be out of date within one legislative session. Budget for ongoing monitoring, and build the geofence as a configuration table with a per-state effective-date column, not as hard-coded logic. [AUDIT ADDITION] As at 14 Sep 2026 Oklahoma (1 Nov 2026) is the ONLY listed prohibition not yet operative — do not stage a launch into that seven-week window.

MOST SWEEPSTAKES BANS REQUIRE THE GAME TO 'SIMULATE CASINO-STYLE GAMBLING', AND A TRIVIA DUEL PROBABLY DOES NOT — BUT DO NOT BUILD ON THAT GAP. It is untested, it is a question of characterisation that a hostile AG will resolve against you, Oklahoma's 'representative of value' definition is drafted broadly enough to reach any dual-currency exchangeable for any chance to win, Iowa's S.F. 2289 is a pure enforcement grant with no definitional limit at all, and California s.337a(a)(6) and Florida s.849.14 close the gap independently of any sweepstakes ban.

MONEY TRANSMISSION IS THE HIDDEN COST CENTRE — BUT CORRECTED, AND THE CORRECTION CUTS IN THE FOUNDER'S FAVOUR FOR MODEL C. State MTL regimes, and the CSBS MTMA definition, generally turn on receiving money FOR TRANSMISSION TO ANOTHER PERSON. Model B — holding one player's stake for payment to another player — squarely raises money transmission and, if required across the country, means licences in 49 states plus DC: fees $500-$10,000 per state, bonds from $10,000 to $500,000 (California scaling to $7m), tangible net worth the greater of $100,000 or 3% of assets, 3-12 months per state and 12-18+ for New York and California. That is a multi-year, seven-figure programme and it is effectively disqualifying for a startup. Model C — operator-funded, fixed, entrant-count-independent prizes paid from the operator's own funds — is frequently NOT transmission to a third party and may fall outside the definition entirely in many states. The brief collapsed the two and called a 49-state programme 'the single largest cost and time line item in the whole plan' for both, which materially overstates the burden for the design it recommends. Get a money-transmission opinion on the threshold question before assuming the programme exists. The MTMA harmonises standards, not licences, and its adopter count as stated in the brief was internally inconsistent and is UNVERIFIED. The safest structure remains never taking custody, via a licensed PSP or sponsor bank.

APP STORE POLICY MAY BE A HARDER GATE THAN STATE LAW. Both Apple and Google require real-money gaming apps to be submitted by the licensed entity and geo-restricted to licensed territories. CORRECTED: the reason is not that no licence exists anywhere — Nevada NRS 463.160 and New Jersey's DGE esports event wagering licence are real categories — but that none of them fits a peer-to-peer mobile trivia app at viable cost or lead time, so there is no licence you can actually show the stores. Model B may simply be unshippable on either store regardless of how the state analysis comes out. Confirm current store policy directly before spending on legal opinions.

THE PRODUCT'S CURRENT MECHANICS ARE THE WORST-CASE FACTS. A 5/7/10-second timer compresses the skill window and amplifies reaction-time variance; randomised question sets introduce a draw-luck element; Expeditions stake at three confidence tiers on rotating question sets, which reads as a wager on an uncertain outcome; and matchmaking determines your opponent. Each of those is a chance input a prosecutor or plaintiff will point to under a material-element test. If real money is ever introduced, the paid path must be redesigned: identical question sets for all entrants, no confidence-tier variance, and a fixed operator-funded prize.

NO STATE OFFERS A COMMERCIALLY VIABLE LICENCE FOR THIS — CORRECTED FROM 'NO STATE LICENSES THIS'. The brief stated a categorical 51-jurisdiction absolute that its own Nevada entry contradicted. Licensure exists in principle: Nevada NRS 463.0152 defines a gambling game as any game played for money with NO skill/chance distinction and NRS 463.160 licenses exactly that, and New Jersey's DGE licenses esports event wagering. What is true is that no state has an OFF-THE-SHELF licence category that fits a peer-to-peer mobile trivia app at viable cost and lead time: the categories that exist are casino, sports wagering, fantasy sports, lottery, charitable gaming and, in a handful of states, esports wagering, and a Nevada non-restricted licence is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar suitability process. The practical conclusion for a startup is unchanged — 'lawful-only-with-licence' is not a path you can fund — but the claim must be stated accurately, because an investor or counsel will find the Nevada contradiction immediately.

[AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL GAMING COMPACTS ARE A STATE-LAYER RISK THE ORIGINAL BRIEF NEVER MENTIONED. Exclusivity provisions in state-tribal compacts in California, Florida, Oklahoma and Connecticut give tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming. Tribal objection has killed products that had a clean reading of the state criminal code, and it arrives through a different channel — compact dispute mechanisms, federal court, and political pressure on the state regulator — so a clean penal-code opinion does not dispose of it. Oklahoma additionally grants tribal operators exclusive online gambling rights. Compact provisions and their reach to a non-casino skill product: UNVERIFIED. Scope the gaming-counsel engagement to cover it.

[AUDIT ADDITION] UNCLAIMED PROPERTY IS A LIVE OBLIGATION FOR THE TWO MODELS THE BRIEF CLEARED AS 'LAWFUL'. Models A and D both accumulate stored value in unredeemed coin and credit balances. Several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as ABANDONED PROPERTY with reporting and remittance duties to the state treasurer after a dormancy period. The brief cleared A and D with no caveat beyond in-app-purchase disclosure. The engineering consequence is immediate even though the legal one is not: you need a server-authoritative per-user balance ledger with last-activity timestamps, which FACT//DUEL's local-only IndexedDB store cannot provide. Per-state thresholds, dormancy periods and whether closed-loop non-redeemable game currency is exempt: UNVERIFIED.

[AUDIT ADDITION] GEOFENCING THE COMPANY IS NOT THE SAME AS PROTECTING THE USER. Several statutes this lane relies on reach the person who PLAYS OR BETS, not only the operator — 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) and Cal. Penal Code s.337a among them. The brief disentangled the two only for Illinois. Whoever writes the terms of service needs to know, per state, whether the block list protects the company, the user, or both, because it determines the refund posture, whether a balance must be returned to a user who played from a prohibited state, and what the product may truthfully tell users about their own exposure. Per-state scope: UNVERIFIED.

[AUDIT ADDITION] THE FREE-ENTRY (AMOE) ROUTE IS THE MOST LEGISLATIVELY TARGETED STRUCTURE IN THE COUNTRY RIGHT NOW. The brief jumped from Model B to Model C without evaluating whether a genuine alternative method of entry would remove the consideration element and open more states — the structure the sweepstakes industry actually uses. It is a real option and leaving it unmapped leaves the strategy space incomplete. But the decisive fact is that the ENTIRE 2025-26 dual-currency ban wave catalogued in this lane exists precisely BECAUSE operators used an AMOE to argue they were not gambling. An AMOE is legitimate for a promotional contest; it is not a safe harbour in 2026, and it does not help at all in states whose prohibition does not turn on consideration (AZ, FL, DE, SD, LA). Cost it before committing; do not adopt it without a per-state opinion. UNVERIFIED as to which states it opens.

regions.name: European Union
regions.posture: There is no EU gambling licence and no EU gambling regulator — the Commission states flatly that there is no sector-specific EU legislation in the field of gambling services — so FACT//DUEL's money product must be licensed (or lawfully structured) state by state across 27 regimes. Model B (staking redeemable for cash) is not launchable as a pan-EU proposition: the EU definitions turn on stake + chance + prize, no member state accepts a dual paid-plus-free entry route as cleansing the paid route, and in the largest markets there is no licence class that fits a player-v-player knowledge stake. Model C (paid-entry knowledge contest) splits the Union three ways, but NOT along the lines the uncorrected brief drew: outside gambling law in Germany and Austria ONLY IF chance does not predominate — and in Germany a paid skill contest that escapes the GlueStV lands in § 33d GewO, which requires its own trade permit (AUDIT ADDITION; online application contested); contested-but-adverse in the Netherlands, where appellate authority has run against skill claims; LICENSABLE, NOT EXEMPT, in Sweden (Spellagen's kombinationsspel expressly covers skill-plus-chance games — the uncorrected brief's placement of Sweden outside gambling law was wrong), Ireland, Italy, Spain, Denmark and Malta; and caught in France because L320-1 CSI bites wherever ANY part of the gain is due to chance — France does not prohibit skill contests as a class, but FACT//DUEL's randomly drawn questions and reflex timers almost certainly put it inside the prohibition. Models A and D need no gambling licence anywhere, CONDITIONALLY: Model A becomes criminal exposure in Belgium if coins buy randomised rewards, and any competitive advantage bought by a Model D subscription converts it into Model C.

verdicts.summary: MODEL A is lawful under every horizontal EU instrument in this lane, and the reason is cleaner than the original brief stated. (1) E-MONEY — CORRECTED. Coins are not electronic money because EMD2 Art 2(2) limb (ii) fails: only FACT//DUEL accepts them, no third party does, and they are not transferable as a separate monetary asset (EBA Q&A 2022_6336). Limb (i) also fails because they are not issued for the purpose of making payment transactions. The invariant to protect is NON-TRANSFERABILITY AND NO THIRD-PARTY ACCEPTANCE — no player-to-player gifting or trading, no priceable secondary market, no acceptance of your coin by any other merchant. The original brief told you that a goodwill cash refund or an account-closure balance return could make you an e-money issuer; the auditor is right that this is wrong, because a refund from you to your own customer involves no third party accepting anything. Consumer-friendly refunds are lawful and in fact partly mandatory. (2) VAT — CORRECTED AND STILL BINDING. A non-EU seller of a digital service to an EU consumer owes VAT at the consumer's member-state rate from the first euro: VAT Directive Art 58 (place of supply), Art 73 (taxable amount), and Art 59c's EUR 10,000 micro-threshold applies only to EU-ESTABLISHED sellers. That conclusion rests on the directive, NOT on CJEU C-472/24. C-472/24 MB 'Zaidimu valiuta' (judgment 5 March 2026) concerned a THIRD-PARTY TRADER reselling RuneScape gold on a secondary market, not a publisher issuing its own currency; the Court held that exchanging real currency for units usable only inside an online game is not exempt under Art 135(1)(e) and is not a voucher under Art 30a, so Art 73 general rules apply. Extending that to a first-party issuer's own coin sale is a reasonable inference, not a holding, and the single-purpose voucher analysis under Art 30a(2) for a first-party issuer was NOT before the Court. Take the conservative position (VAT at sale of coins) but know it is inference. (3) WITHDRAWAL — RE-LABELLED. CRD Art 9 gives a 14-day withdrawal right on the coin purchase contract. The CPC Network's further position — that in-game virtual currency is NOT itself digital content, so the Art 16(1)(m) waiver cannot extinguish that right, and unspent coins must be cash-refundable — is SOFT LAW that Video Games Europe and EGDF dispute and on which German courts have gone the other way (properly-run waivers upheld). Build the refund path because it is cheap and because it is the stated enforcement posture; do not describe it as settled law. (4) PRICING / UCPD — RE-LABELLED. Real-money price display at the undiscounted bundle rate, exact-amount coin purchase, no stacked currencies, and spending-off-by-default parental controls are CPC Key Principles positions built on UCPD Arts 5-9 and CRD Art 6(1)(e). The underlying UCPD misleading-omission analysis is real law; the specific prescriptions are the Network's reading of it. (5) AUDIT ADDITIONS. Directive (EU) 2019/770 (Digital Content Directive) is the core contract-law instrument here and was missing entirely: Arts 6-8 conformity, Arts 14-18 remedies and reimbursement on termination, and critically Art 19, which governs when you may MODIFY digital content or a digital service during continuous supply and gives the consumer a free termination right where a modification adversely affects access or use — that, not UCTD Art 3 alone, is what constrains post-launch coin rebalancing. CRD Art 8(2)'s 'order with obligation to pay' button labelling applies to EVERY coin-purchase button, not just a subscription confirm; non-compliance means the consumer is NOT BOUND by the contract, i.e. revenue reversal. Directive 2000/31/EC Arts 5, 6 and 10 impose provider-identification and commercial-communication duties alongside CRD Art 6, and its Art 3 country-of-origin principle gives a non-EU-established provider nothing. Rome I Regulation (EC) 593/2008 Art 6(1)-(2) is why all of this binds you at all: a trader directing activities to a member state is subject to the mandatory consumer-protection law of the consumer's habitual residence, and a choice-of-law clause cannot take it away; Brussels Ia Regulation (EU) 1215/2012 Art 18 lets the consumer sue at home. None of this makes Model A unlawful; all of it makes an unmodified launch unlawful.
