Assume 27 sets of mandatory rules apply to everything that cannot be contracted away.

[AUDIT ADDITION] COLLECTIVE REDRESS IS THE REALISTIC ENFORCEMENT VECTOR AND THE ORIGINAL BRIEF NEVER MENTIONED IT. Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on representative actions has applied since 25 June 2023: qualified entities can bring cross-border collective redress for infringements of the CRD, UCPD, UCTD, DCD and the GDPR. For a coin economy that will demonstrably reach minors, a qualified-entity action is at least as likely as a regulator action and carries damages rather than commitments.

[AUDIT ADDITION] DIRECTIVE (EU) 2019/770 ART 19 IS THE HARD LIMIT ON REBALANCING A PAID COIN ECONOMY. The original brief attributed this constraint to UCTD Art 3 and the CPC Principles alone. DCD Art 19 is hard law: modification of a continuously-supplied digital service requires a contractual basis, a valid reason, no extra cost and advance notice on a durable medium, and where the change adversely affects access or use the consumer may TERMINATE FREE and claim reimbursement under Arts 16-18. Design the economy on the assumption that you cannot devalue or withdraw what people paid for.

[AUDIT ADDITION] THE EUROPEAN ACCESSIBILITY ACT IS A DELAYED-FUSE COST. Directive (EU) 2019/882 has applied since 28 June 2025 to consumer-facing e-commerce services. You are exempt only as a microenterprise service provider (Art 4(5)); the exemption evaporates at 10 staff or EUR 2m turnover — i.e. exactly when a monetised launch succeeds. Retrofitting WCAG-level accessibility into a timer-driven, heavily animated, audio-cued game is expensive. Build the checkout accessibly now.

[CORRECTED] THE EU-US DATA PRIVACY FRAMEWORK COULD FALL AGAIN MID-BUILD. It is valid today. The General Court dismissed the challenge in Case T-553/23 Latombe v Commission on 3 September 2025; the appeal was lodged 31 October 2025 and is pending as Case C-703/25 P (case number corroborated by independent sources and retained). The original brief's additional claims of 'no hearing date announced as at mid-2026' and 'Microsoft granted leave to intervene on 29 June 2026' are UNCORROBORATED and removed. The CJEU killed both predecessor frameworks. Do not design a US-processor architecture with no fallback: SCCs plus transfer impact assessments in every US vendor contract NOW, and know which processors you could move to EU regions.

[CORRECTED] PSD3/PSR WILL RESHUFFLE THE PERIMETER RIGHT AFTER YOU LAUNCH — AND IT REPEALS EMD2. Provisional political agreement 27 November 2025 is corroborated; the brief's '23 April 2026 final compromise texts' date is not, and is removed. The cited source puts expected OJ publication at end of Q2 2026 and PSR application at 18 months after entry into force (payee-name verification at 24), not ~21 months. MATERIAL AND PREVIOUSLY OMITTED: PSD3 REPEALS EMD2 OUTRIGHT; existing EMI authorisations survive only 24 months after entry into force (extendable to 30) with a MANDATORY RE-APPLICATION. So an EMI licence obtained for Model B in 2027 would need re-papering almost immediately. Build Model B only with counsel tracking the PSR text.

BETAAL GARANT IS A THINNER SHIELD THAN IT LOOKS. C-51/25 (16 July 2026) is genuinely helpful — ancillary fund transfers serving a primary non-payment service are outside PSD2 — but practitioners describe it as fact-specific and confined, it turned partly on the intermediary not holding the payer's payment account, it did NOT address money remittance, and further CJEU references are pending. Holding named per-player balances is the fact most likely to defeat the ancillary argument. Do not let anyone treat this judgment as a licence substitute.

THE DIGITAL FAIRNESS ACT IS A KNOWN FUTURE RESET AND EVERY TIMELINE CLAIM ABOUT IT IS PRESS REPORTING. A proposal expected H2 2026 covering dark patterns, addictive design, loot boxes and virtual currencies will land on this exact product category. The cheap insurance is to build the real-money price display, the exact-amount coin purchase and the no-randomised-paid-rewards rule now, so the DFA is a documentation exercise rather than a rebuild.

A SINGLE FEATURE CAN FLIP YOU INTO THE FULL DSA ONLINE-PLATFORM REGIME. Today you are probably not even an intermediary; with accounts you are probably a hosting service (Arts 11, 12, 14, 16 — NOT Art 15, which Art 15(2) disapplies for micro/small enterprises); with public leaderboards carrying user-authored text, global chat, or user-generated question packs you become an 'online platform' and acquire Arts 20-28, including the Art 28 minor-protection duty. Put a DSA scoping gate in the product review process for any social feature.

[CONTESTED] THE AI ACT OMNIBUS DATES IN THE ORIGINAL BRIEF ARE UNCORROBORATED. The claim that the AI Omnibus was 'adopted by Council 29 June 2026, published in the OJ 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026' matches no reachable source; the brief's own citation records only political agreement 6 May 2026 and Council confirmation 13 May 2026, with adoption and OJ publication 'expected before 2 August 2026'. Treat the dates as contested and verify the OJ citation before relying on any deferral. The substance holds: Annex III stand-alone high-risk deferred to 2 December 2027, Annex I embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028, Art 5 prohibitions NOT deferred and in force since 2 February 2025, Art 50 transparency obligations live from 2 August 2026, and a new Art 5 prohibition (nudifiers/CSAM) added with a transitional period to 2 December 2026.

TODAY'S DEMO COINS ARE OUTSIDE ALL OF THIS — AND THAT IS A ONE-WAY DOOR. Footnote 2 of the CPC Key Principles expressly excludes in-game currencies obtainable solely through gameplay and not purchasable with real-world money. FACT//DUEL's current demo coins and Expedition points sit in that carve-out. The moment a purchase path exists, the entire consumer-law layer switches on for the design, not just for the new purchase flow — including the price-display and no-stacked-currency principles that constrain how points and coins may relate to each other.

regions.name: India
regions.posture: India bans cash-out staking outright and leaves purchased-coin staking genuinely UNSETTLED. s.5 of the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 (in force 1 May 2026) criminalises offering an "online money game" — s.2(1)(g), "irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both" — with 3 years' imprisonment, ₹1 crore fine, cognizable and non-bailable, directors personally liable, and express extraterritorial reach over operators outside India. MODEL B (cash/prize redemption) and MODEL C (paid entry for an announced prize pool) are squarely caught and are criminal offences: do not ship them. MODEL D (subscription) is expressly blessed by s.2(1)(i)(ii). MODEL A (buy coins for cosmetics/entries, never convertible to money) is the only lawful route to taking money for a duel-shaped product — BUT whether purchased, NON-CASHABLE coins staked player-v-player are themselves an "online money game" is CONTESTED and untested. There is no OGAI determination and no judgment on the point; the weight of published 2026 Indian commentary reads a non-convertible in-game coin as falling OUTSIDE "other stakes" in s.2(1)(j) and inside "online social game", while a plain-meaning reading of the "which is purchased" limb would catch it. Treat this as a live legal risk to be priced and opinioned on by Indian counsel, not as a settled answer in either direction — the previous version of this lane asserted it as settled criminality and that assertion is withdrawn.

verdicts.verdict: lawful in its pure form; CONTESTED if purchased coins are staked player-v-player
verdicts.summary: Model A as defined — money in, cosmetics and prize-free entries out, nothing convertible back to money or to a prize of value — sits outside s.2(1)(g) and inside "online social game" in s.2(1)(i). s.2(1)(g) defines an online money game as one "played by a user by paying fees, depositing money or other stakes in expectation of winning which entails monetary AND other enrichment in return of money or other stakes". CORRECTION (audit, verified verbatim against Bar & Bench's quotation of the section): the conjunction is "and", not "or". There is therefore a serious argument that monetary enrichment is a NECESSARY component of the winning limb, and that winning further non-monetary in-game credit alone does not satisfy it. The earlier version of this lane relied on a disjunctive reading it never disclosed; that reliance is withdrawn. s.2(1)(i) permits a game that (i) does not involve staking or participation with expectation of winning monetary gain, (ii) "may allow access through payment of a subscription fee or one-time access fee, provided that such payment is not in the nature of a stake or wager", and (iii) is offered solely for entertainment, recreation or skill-development; limb (ii) is permissive, not an exhaustive list of lawful payments. The 2026 Rules' five-factor determination test [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict] turns on whether rewards or in-game assets "can be transferred, redeemed, monetised or used outside the game environment"; purely cosmetic, non-tradeable items with no external market sit on the permitted side. THE CONTESTED POINT — STAKING PURCHASED COINS. s.2(1)(j) defines "other stakes" as "anything recognised as equivalent or convertible to money and includes credits, coins, token or objects ... whether it is real or virtual, which is purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means or as part of, or in relation to, an online game". This lane now adopts ONE construction consistently (audit defect: the prior version read the definition as self-sufficient where that produced an alarming answer and as conjunctive where that produced a convenient one): the CONJUNCTIVE reading — the thing must be BOTH "recognised as equivalent or convertible to money" AND purchased/acquired. On that reading, coins that are non-transferable, non-redeemable, have no secondary market and no external convertibility are NOT "other stakes", even when bought with real money — and a duel staking them is not an online money game. That is also the reading taken by the most directly on-point published 2026 analysis (respawn.outlookindia.com, "Pocket casinos: how mobile games are exposing PROGA's loopholes"), which concludes that a game "which takes real money and returns dice rolls and stickers, almost certainly falls within PROGA's definition of an online social game". The contrary reading — that "which is purchased" is a self-sufficient inclusive limb, so any purchased virtual coin is a stake with or without cash-out — is available on the words and is the reading a regulator taking a policy view would reach for. NEITHER reading has been tested by OGAI or by a court. PRACTICAL POSITION: the two-ledger architecture (purchased currency → cosmetics only; free, non-purchasable currency → duel stakes) is no longer presented as legally compelled, but it remains the design that makes the question moot, and it is the cheapest way to buy out an unquantifiable criminal-law risk in a jurisdiction where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable. Recommend shipping it. TWO CONDITIONS ARE NOT CONTESTED AND ARE LOAD-BEARING: (1) the word "entries" in the model description is dangerous — coins buying entry to any contest with a prize of VALUE converts Model A into Model C, which is unlawful; entries must be to prize-free play only. (2) No transferability, no gifting, no secondary market, no account trading — any of these creates external convertibility and collapses the conjunctive defence. Registration is not required (online social games are registrable voluntarily only), but a voluntary determination application to OGAI is available and is the only route to a written classification — see the checklist for its costs, including the registration-triggered India data-residency duty and the exposure of putting a named foreign operator in front of the regulator.
verdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.2(1)(g), 2(1)(i), 2(1)(j), 5 — section numbers and quotations verified against the MeitY-published primary text. Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, five-factor determination test — [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]. Both in force 1 May 2026 (Rules notified 22 April 2026, Gazette of India ref CG-DL-E-22042026-271974; G.S.R. number UNVERIFIED). Construction of s.2(1)(j) as applied to purchased non-cashable coins: CONTESTED, no determination or judgment found.

verdicts.summary: Flatly criminal, and this verdict does not depend on any contested construction. Winnings redeemable for cash or prizes of value satisfy s.2(1)(g) on any reading: the user deposits money or other stakes, and wins "monetary and other enrichment" — monetary enrichment is present, so the conjunctive reading of the winning limb (which rescues Model A) gives Model B no help at all. The skill/chance distinction is statutorily abolished ("irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both"), so the old Indian jurisprudence on rummy and fantasy sports is dead for online play. CORRECTION (audit): the prior version said there is "no sweepstakes doctrine, no dual-currency carve-out and no alternative-method-of-entry defence anywhere in Indian law". The first half stands — those are US constructs and there is no PROGA carve-out for them. The claim that Indian law has nothing in this space is wrong: free-entry and skill-based prize competitions are governed by the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 and by State prize-competition and lottery legislation, which constrain rather than enable any AMOE-style redesign. See the checklist item and subdivision rows; scope of the 1955 Act as applied to an online quiz is UNVERIFIED. CONSEQUENCES: s.5 prohibits offering, and equally "aid, abet, induce or otherwise indulge or engage in the offering"; s.9(1) — up to 3 years' imprisonment or a fine up to ₹1 crore or both; s.9(4) — a second conviction carries a MINIMUM 3 years (up to 5) and a minimum ₹1 crore fine (up to ₹2 crore); s.10 makes ss.5 and 7 COGNIZABLE AND NON-BAILABLE, so arrest without warrant and no bail as of right; s.11 makes every person in charge of the business, and any consenting or conniving director/manager/officer, personally liable (independent and non-executive directors not in actual decision-making are carved out); s.16 lets authorised officers enter and search "any place, whether physical or digital", arrest without warrant and override access controls. ADVERTISING IS A SEPARATE OFFENCE: s.6 bans any advertisement that "directly or indirectly promotes or induces any person to play any online money game", punishable under s.9(2) with up to 2 years or ₹50 lakh or both; note s.6 is NOT listed in s.10, so it is not cognizable/non-bailable — most commentary gets this wrong. FACILITATING IS A SEPARATE OFFENCE: s.7 bars any bank, financial institution "or any other person facilitating financial transactions" from processing payment for an online money gaming service, punishable under s.9(3) with up to 3 years or ₹1 crore — which is why Indian PSPs refuse anything that smells of staking. OFFSHORE OPERATION IS NOT AN ESCAPE: s.1(2) states the Act "extends to the whole of India and also applies to online money gaming service offered within the territory of India or operated from outside the territory of India", and the long title expressly targets services operating "from foreign jurisdictions". CORRECTION (audit, contested): the prior version asserted that "s.14 lets blocking notwithstanding s.69A of the IT Act 2000". That override is UNVERIFIED — the provision was not quoted. PRS's summary describes s.14 as empowering the Central Government to block information relating to online money gaming services; whether it overrides s.69A or operates THROUGH the s.69A procedure and the 2009 Blocking Rules is material, because it decides whether the s.69A safeguards (committee, hearing, reasoned order) attach to a blocking order against the app. Treat as CONTESTED. Enforcement reality is unchanged either way: 8,376 betting/gambling URLs blocked as at 28 March 2026, and OGAI's first advisory of 29 July 2026 directed app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos, banks, social media intermediaries, OTT platforms and ad agencies to delist apps, block payments and pull ads. The route against a foreign founder is app-store removal, payment blocking and ISP blocking within days — not litigation.
verdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.1(2), 2(1)(g), 2(1)(j), 5, 6, 7, 9(1)-(5), 10, 11, 16 — verified against MeitY primary text; s.14 scope CONTESTED/UNVERIFIED. Prize Competitions Act, 1955 and State prize-competition/lottery legislation — applicability to online quiz UNVERIFIED (audit addition). In force 1 May 2026.

verdicts.verdict: unlawful — criminal; no licence exists to buy
verdicts.summary: Unlawful, and the fixed, operator-funded, announced prize pool does not help. s.2(1)(g) requires only (a) paying fees, depositing money or other stakes and (b) an expectation of winning entailing enrichment. A fixed entry fee is squarely "paying fees"; an announced CASH-or-value prize supplies monetary enrichment, so the "monetary and other enrichment" conjunction does not rescue Model C either. Nothing in the definition turns on whether the pool varies with entrant count, on peer-to-peer versus house-banked structure, or on skill ("irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both"). Secondary commentary on the Act is explicit that trivia and quiz contests charging entry fees and distributing cash prizes are banned, alongside fantasy sports, rummy and poker. THERE IS EXACTLY ONE EXIT AND IT IS NOT REALISTICALLY AVAILABLE TO A TRIVIA APP: s.2(1)(g) carves out e-sports, and s.2(1)(c) permits a game that (i) "is played as part of multi-sports events", (ii) involves organised competitive events in multiplayer formats under predefined rules, (iii) "is duly recognised under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, and registered with the Authority or agency under section 3", (iv) has its outcome determined solely by skill, (v) "may include payment of registration or participation fees solely for the purpose of entering the competition or covering administrative costs and may include performance-based prize money for the player", and (vi) "shall not involve the placing of bets, wagers or any other stakes by any person, whether or not such person is a participant". Limb (iii) is the killer: recognition under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025) must be obtained FIRST, and a mobile trivia app is not a multi-sports-event discipline and will not obtain it. CORRECTION (audit, defect withdrawn): the prior version stated that "OGAI cannot make an e-sport determination without the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports member present and concurring". NO SOURCE SUPPORTS A MEMBER-SPECIFIC CONCURRENCE OR VETO. The claim is withdrawn as probably invented. OGAI's actual decision-making rules, as reported by SCC Online and Bar & Bench, are ordinary: a Chairperson plus six members, quorum of at least half the total members (online or in person), decisions by majority vote, Chairperson's (or presiding member's) casting vote in a tie, with urgent decisions permitted by written order notified to members within 3 days. A Joint Secretary from the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports is an ex officio member — membership is not a veto. The conclusion is unaffected: NSGA recognition remains the blocker. E-sport registration with OGAI is then mandatory [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict] (Bar & Bench places mandatory e-sports registration at rule 12(1)(b) and permissible e-sports payments at rule 9, which conflicts with the sources placing the five-factor determination test at rule 9). 90-day target; certificate validity reported as up to 10 years. I am deliberately NOT calling this "licence-required": there is no licence a founder can buy. Treat paid-entry contests as closed in India.
verdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.2(1)(c), 2(1)(g), 5, 9(1) — verified against MeitY primary text. National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025) (recognition precondition in s.2(1)(c)(iii)). Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, e-sports registration and certificate validity — [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]. In force 1 May 2026.

verdicts.summary: Expressly lawful — the one model the statute affirmatively blesses. s.2(1)(i)(ii) provides that an online social game "may allow access through payment of a subscription fee or one-time access fee, provided that such payment is not in the nature of a stake or wager". A recurring fee for features or cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value sits inside the permitted category and outside s.5. CONDITIONS: the subscription must not buy entry to, or advantage in, any prize-bearing contest; subscriber-only currency must not be stakeable; there must be no cash-out, no transfer and no external monetisation of anything the subscription unlocks (the reward-monetisation factor in the determination test). Registration is NOT required — online social games are registrable voluntarily, and the Central Government has not, on the sources available, notified any category of online social game into mandatory registration (UNVERIFIED as at 14 September 2026; the item most likely to change). CORRECTION (audit): the prior version called a voluntary determination application "the cheapest insurance available" without disclosing its costs. It is still worth considering, but registration is reported to be what switches on an India data-residency obligation (retention of traffic data, metadata and related information on computer resources located in India) for registered social games and e-sports — UNVERIFIED, could not be corroborated from the sources reachable, but if true it is a direct engineering and hosting cost caused by the recommendation itself. Filing also puts a named (possibly foreign) operator in front of the regulator, and whether a provider with no Indian presence can even file is UNVERIFIED. CORRECTION (audit): the prior version also treated India obligations as beginning "at the first rupee". They do not. The 2026 Rules' social-game safeguards (age verification, parental controls, time limits, fair-play monitoring, grievance redressal — UNVERIFIED, audit addition) and the DPDP child-data regime attach to the CURRENT FREE PRODUCT wherever it has Indian users. Do not defer India work until monetisation. Tax and data obligations apply in full: 18% GST on the subscription (OIDAR registration from the first Indian rupee if supplied from outside India), and DPDP Act 2023 s.9 child-data duties, which are the real engineering cost. Note also that determinations are reported to bind only your product and only while the model is unchanged [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict] — any move toward staking is a material change requiring notification and triggering reclassification.
verdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), s.2(1)(i)(ii) read with s.5 — verified against MeitY primary text. Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026 — [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]. Tax: Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (OIDAR). Data: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 22 of 2023), s.9; Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (gazette reference CONTESTED — see corrections).

subdivisions.name: All other States
subdivisions.status: No State route; PROGA governs uniformly
subdivisions.detail: PROGA applies to the whole of India, so the model verdicts do not vary by State. The residual State layer to check with counsel is (a) State prize-competition and lottery legislation, which constrains any free-entry/AMOE or skill-prize design (see checklist), and (b) the Public Gambling Act, 1867 and its State adaptations, which continue to govern OFFLINE activity. Neither creates a route to market for Models B or C.
subdivisions.authority: PROG Act ss.1(2), 5, 18; Prize Competitions Act, 1955; Public Gambling Act, 1867 and State adaptations. Scope UNVERIFIED

subdivisions.status: Historic skill-game licensing regime; status after PROGA UNVERIFIED — do NOT treat as a route to market
subdivisions.detail: Nagaland is commonly cited as one of the few States that historically licensed online games of skill. Whether any such licence survives PROGA, and whether it could authorise anything PROGA s.5 prohibits, is UNVERIFIED and on the face of s.18 highly doubtful — PROGA abolishes the skill/chance distinction for online play, which is the foundation such licences rested on. Do not plan a Model B or C launch around a State skill-game licence.

subdivisions.name: Union of India (central law — the operative layer)
subdivisions.status: Governing. Models B and C criminal; Model D lawful; Model A lawful with one CONTESTED limb
subdivisions.detail: PROGA and the 2026 Rules are CENTRAL law and apply uniformly across every State and Union Territory. s.18 gives the Act overriding effect to the extent of any inconsistency with other law. All model verdicts in this lane are decided at this level; the State rows below exist only to answer the residual question of whether any State exposure survives. AUDIT NOTE: the prior version of this lane carried ZERO subdivision rows. These rows are an audit addition responding to the omission of the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 and State prize-competition/lottery law.
subdivisions.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.1(2), 5, 18; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026 (in force 1 May 2026)

subdivisions.detail: PROGA extends to the whole of India. The only UT-specific fact of operational relevance is that OGAI's head office is in the National Capital Territory of Delhi, which is where a voluntary determination application and any appeal to the Secretary, MeitY would be directed.
subdivisions.authority: PROG Act s.1(2); OGAI constituted as an attached office of MeitY with head office in NCT of Delhi

checklist.item: DO NOT launch Model B or Model C in India — hard geo-block India for any cash-out, redemption or prize-of-value feature (IP geolocation + app store country availability + payment BIN/country checks + account country lock)
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; enforced by Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), MeitY
checklist.prerequisite: None — this is the gating decision
checklist.notes: s.1(2) of the PROG Act reaches services "operated from outside the territory of India", so a US or EU entity serving Indian users commits the s.5 offence. s.11 makes directors personally liable. Geo-blocking must be real, not a terms-of-service disclaimer; OGAI's 29 July 2026 advisory went to app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos and banks, so the realistic failure mode is overnight delisting and payment blocking, not a lawsuit. CORRECTED SCOPE (audit): this item is now about cash-out and prizes of value, which are unarguably caught. Purchased-coin staking WITHOUT cash-out is a separate, CONTESTED question — see the next item.

checklist.item: DECIDE, with Indian counsel and in writing, whether purchased coins may be staked player-v-player at all — this is the one genuinely unsettled India question and it must be priced, not assumed
checklist.issuer: Indian counsel; ultimately OGAI (determination) or a court
checklist.leadTime: Before enabling any purchase flow for India
checklist.prerequisite: Final coin-economy spec
checklist.notes: AUDIT CORRECTION — REPLACES THE PRIOR "DECISIVE RISK" FRAMING. The previous version of this lane asserted that purchased, non-cashable coins staked player-v-player are automatically an online money game and that the escrow duel "flips from lawful to criminal" the instant coins become purchasable. That is withdrawn as overstated. The question turns on s.2(1)(j): "anything recognised as equivalent or convertible to money and includes credits, coins, token or objects ... which is purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means or as part of, or in relation to, an online game". On the CONJUNCTIVE reading this lane now adopts consistently, a non-transferable, non-redeemable coin with no external market is NOT "other stakes" and the duel is lawful; this is also the reading of the most on-point published 2026 analysis (Outlook/Respawn, "Pocket casinos"), which concludes such a product "almost certainly falls within PROGA's definition of an online social game". On the aggressive reading, "which is purchased" is self-sufficient and the duel is caught. Reinforcing the permissive side: s.2(1)(g)'s winning limb reads "monetary AND other enrichment" (conjunction verified verbatim), so winning further non-monetary in-game credit alone may not satisfy it. NO OGAI determination and NO judgment resolves this. Reasonable Indian counsel currently differ. Get the opinion before you build.

checklist.item: Architect two hard-separated currency ledgers: PURCHASED currency (cosmetics only, never stakeable, never winnable, never transferable) and FREE currency (duel stakes only, never purchasable, no cash value)
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; classified by OGAI under the five-factor determination test [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]
checklist.prerequisite: Decision to monetise Model A; outcome of the counsel opinion above
checklist.notes: CORRECTED STATUS (audit): this is a RISK-ELIMINATING design choice, not a legally compelled one — the prior version presented it as compelled by a settled reading of s.2(1)(j) that is in fact contested. It remains the recommendation, because it makes the contested question moot in a jurisdiction where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable and directors are personally liable, and because it costs engineering time rather than an unquantifiable criminal-law exposure. If you build it: beware "or by indirect means" in s.2(1)(j) — bundling free stake-currency into a cosmetic purchase, or granting it on subscription, arguably re-taints it. Remove any gifting, trading or account-transfer path regardless of which ledger design you choose: external convertibility is the one factor that defeats the permissive reading on its own terms.

checklist.item: Remove or India-gate coin-purchase entry into Expeditions and any paid-entry event with a PRIZE OF VALUE; prize-free entries and non-purchasable points staking are the safe side
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; classified by OGAI under the five-factor determination test [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]
checklist.prerequisite: Ledger decision above
checklist.notes: "Coins buy entries" converts Model A into Model C — which is unlawful — if the entry leads to a prize of value. This limb is NOT contested and is the sharpest single India constraint on Model A. Expedition points as currently designed (minted by play, not purchasable, not convertible) sit outside s.2(1)(j) on the conjunctive reading this lane adopts throughout: they are neither "recognised as equivalent or convertible to money" nor purchased. Note this is the SAME construction applied to purchased coins two items above — the prior version of this lane applied the conjunctive reading here and a self-sufficient reading there, which the audit correctly flagged as incoherent.

checklist.item: Ship the 2026 Rules' USER-SAFETY DUTIES FOR ONLINE SOCIAL GAMES — age verification, parental controls, session/time limits, fair-play monitoring and a grievance-redressal mechanism — on the LAWFUL models and on the current free product
checklist.issuer: Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), MeitY
checklist.appliesTo: A, D (and the current free product)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — treat as live now that the Rules are in force (1 May 2026)
checklist.prerequisite: Any India availability, monetised or not
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION — MISSING FROM THE PRIOR CHECKLIST ENTIRELY. The audit reports that the 2026 Rules impose age verification, parental controls, time limits, fair-play monitoring and grievance redressal on ONLINE SOCIAL GAMES GENERALLY — i.e. on Models A and D, the two lawful models — not only on money games or registered games. UNVERIFIED: I could not corroborate the scope or the rule numbers from the secondary sources reachable (SCC Online, Bar & Bench, Legal500 and ipleaders all summarise the money-game prohibition and the registration architecture without enumerating affirmative duties for permitted categories), and the gazette text of the Rules was not obtained. This is the single most consequential gap in the prior version: a founder working the old checklist would have shipped Model A or D into India believing there were no India-specific gaming obligations at all beyond tax and data. Verify against the gazette text before launch and budget engineering for it.

checklist.item: Establish the APPEAL ROUTE against an adverse OGAI determination, cessation direction or blocking order before you need it
checklist.issuer: Appellate Authority — reported as the Secretary, MeitY; thereafter High Court writ jurisdiction
checklist.leadTime: 30 days from the decision to file (reported); 30 days for disposal (reported)
checklist.prerequisite: An adverse determination or direction
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION — the prior version stated that the final Rules "dropped the Grievance Appellate Committee tier" and then gave no appeal path at all. That statement is WITHDRAWN as fabricated: it is contradicted by the brief's own sources. Bar & Bench reports appeals against Online Gaming Authority decisions going to the Secretary, MeitY as Appellate Authority, with 30 days to file and disposal targeted within 30 days of receipt; Mondaq reports "30-day timelines for Authority and Appellate Authority decisions"; ipleaders describes a tiered route — platform grievance officer, then OGAI adjudication, then final appeal to Secretary MeitY, then High Court writ. Rule numbers UNVERIFIED and conflicting (ipleaders puts grievance in Part V; Legal500 cites rule 20 for user grievance appeals). Given that enforcement is fast, intermediary-led and happens BEFORE any hearing, this route is the founder's only remedy and must be identified in advance.

checklist.item: File a voluntary determination / classification application with the Online Gaming Authority of India to obtain written confirmation that the product is an "online social game" and not an "online money game" — but price its two hidden costs first
checklist.issuer: Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), attached office of MeitY, head office NCT of Delhi
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED — secondary sources say the fee is published on the OGAI portal; amount not confirmed; ogai.gov.in returned 502 from this environment
checklist.leadTime: 90 days from a complete application (statutory target, "as far as practicable"); the clock resets on each request for clarification
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec, revenue model description, user safety features, grievance mechanism, terms of use
checklist.notes: Optional, not mandatory: registration of online social games is voluntary and no category has been notified into mandatory registration on the sources available as at 14 September 2026 (UNVERIFIED). CORRECTED (audit): the prior version called this "the cheapest insurance available" with no downside disclosed. Two costs it omitted. (1) DATA RESIDENCY: registration is reported to switch on an India data-localisation obligation — see the next item. (2) EXPOSURE AND ELIGIBILITY: filing puts a named, possibly foreign, operator in front of the regulator with what this lane elsewhere calls the highest-scrutiny design you could ship into India; whether a provider with NO Indian presence can file at all, and what the point-of-contact / India-resident-officer requirement does to that, is UNVERIFIED. Also note: a favourable determination is reported to bind only your product and only while the model is unchanged [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]. Secondary sources place determination at rule 9, application at rule 8 or 12, the 90-day timeline at rule 10 and certificate validity up to 10 years at rule 14(2) — all INDICATIVE; Bar & Bench conflicts by assigning rule 9 to permissible e-sports payments.

checklist.item: Budget for INDIA DATA LOCALISATION if you register: retention of traffic data, metadata and related information on computer resources located in India
checklist.issuer: Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), MeitY
checklist.prerequisite: A decision to register or to seek a determination that leads to registration
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION. The audit reports that providers of REGISTERED online social games and e-sports must retain traffic data, metadata and related information on computer resources located in India. UNVERIFIED — I could not corroborate this from the secondary sources reachable and the gazette text was not obtained (the prior version listed a "rule 17 data retention" only inside its uncertain section). If correct, it is a direct, previously undisclosed cost consequence of this lane's own recommendation to file for voluntary determination/registration: you would be moving from an ordinary global hosting posture to an India-resident data estate. Verify against the gazette text BEFORE filing, not after.

checklist.item: Do NOT pursue e-sport registration unless the product is genuinely a multi-sports-event discipline
checklist.issuer: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (recognition) then OGAI (registration)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — NSGA recognition must be obtained first and that time is excluded from OGAI's 90-day clock
checklist.prerequisite: Recognition under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025)
checklist.notes: s.2(1)(c)(iii) makes NSGA recognition a precondition, and a trivia app will not clear s.2(1)(c)(i) ("played as part of multi-sports events"). CORRECTED (audit): the prior version's added claim that "OGAI cannot make an e-sport determination without the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports member present and concurring" is WITHDRAWN — no source supports a member-specific concurrence or veto. OGAI's reported decision rules are ordinary: Chairperson plus six members, quorum of at least half the total members (online or in person), majority vote, Chairperson's casting vote on a tie, urgent decisions by written order notified to members within 3 days. A Joint Secretary from Youth Affairs & Sports is an ex officio member; membership is not a veto. The conclusion is unchanged — NSGA recognition is the blocker. Listed here only so the founder does not waste months on it. Bar & Bench places mandatory e-sports registration at rule 12(1)(b) and permissible e-sports payments at rule 9; [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]

checklist.item: Register for GST as an OIDAR supplier (Form GST REG-10) if the selling entity is outside India and takes money from Indian consumers
checklist.issuer: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) / GSTN
checklist.cost: No government filing fee; professional fees UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Foreign selling entity; any supply to an unregistered Indian recipient
checklist.notes: Mandatory from the first transaction — there is no turnover threshold for non-resident OIDAR suppliers. Rate 18% IGST on subscriptions and in-app purchases. Monthly return GSTR-5A due by the 20th of the following month. A supplier with no physical presence in India must appoint an Indian representative for compliance. If you sell exclusively through Apple App Store / Google Play billing the storefront may handle Indian GST — UNVERIFIED, confirm with each store before relying on it.

checklist.item: Register for GST (Form GST REG-01) if you incorporate an Indian entity
checklist.issuer: CBIC / GSTN
checklist.prerequisite: Indian entity incorporation, PAN
checklist.notes: 18% on subscriptions and cosmetic in-app purchases as an online service. Note the 40% GST slab applies to "online money gaming" on the full face value of deposits (reported from 22 September 2025, 56th GST Council) — there is no lawful way to use that slab now that s.5 bans the underlying activity, so treat 40% as a marker of how the state views the category rather than a business option. Exact SAC classification for cosmetic in-app purchases as distinct from subscriptions: UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: Use an RBI-authorised payment aggregator; for a foreign merchant collecting from Indian users, use a Payment Aggregator – Cross Border (PA-CB) authorised entity, or route through app-store billing
checklist.issuer: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
checklist.prerequisite: Entity and GST position settled
checklist.notes: CORRECTED (audit — the prior version's citation here was fabricated in three respects and is withdrawn). (1) INSTRUMENT TITLE: the prior version cited "Reserve Bank of India (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025, dated 15 September 2025". The inserted words "Regulation of" could not be confirmed on RBI's Master Directions or notifications pages, and neither could the 15 September 2025 date; the framework is understood to be titled "Reserve Bank of India (Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025" — TITLE AND DATE UNVERIFIED, check against RBI's own site before citing. (2) ACCOUNT TERMINOLOGY: "Outward Collection Account" is not RBI terminology. The PA-CB framework uses the IMPORT COLLECTION ACCOUNT (ICA) for the leg where Indian buyers pay a foreign merchant — which is your leg — and the EXPORT COLLECTION ACCOUNT (ECA) for the reverse. (3) CAP: the ₹25 lakh per-transaction figure derives from the October 2023 PA-CB circular's per-unit import cap and its survival into the 2025 consolidation is UNVERIFIED. DO NOT PLAN PAYMENT ARCHITECTURE AGAINST THE OLD LABELS OR THAT CAP. What stands: you do not need your own authorisation, you need an authorised partner; and s.7 of the PROG Act criminalises any person facilitating payment for an online money gaming service, which is why Indian PSPs will refuse anything that smells of staking.

checklist.item: Build DPDP child-data compliance: age assurance with real verification, verifiable parental consent for under-18s, and a hard switch that disables behavioural tracking, profiling and targeted advertising for any child user
checklist.issuer: Data Protection Board of India / MeitY
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D (and the current free product)
checklist.cost: Engineering cost; penalty exposure up to ₹200 crore for s.9 breaches and up to ₹250 crore for security-safeguard failures
checklist.prerequisite: Any processing of personal data of Indian users
checklist.notes: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 22 of 2023) treats everyone under 18 as a child. s.9(1) requires verifiable parental consent; s.9(3) prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising DIRECTED AT children. CORRECTED (audit): the prior version called s.9(3) "an absolute bar, not a consent-waivable one". The second half is right — consent cannot cure it. "Absolute" is wrong: s.9(4) empowers the Central Government to exempt classes of data fiduciaries, or processing for prescribed purposes, from BOTH s.9(1) and s.9(3), and the DPDP Rules 2025 exercise that power (reported at the Fourth Schedule). The exemptions are unlikely to reach a quiz game, but the architecture matters if you are testing whether a narrow exemption is available. CORRECTED (audit): the prior version's conclusion that "the cheapest compliant answer is a genuine 18+ gate for India" is WITHDRAWN. An 18+ gate is not a DPDP exit — the DPDP Rules 2025 require a data fiduciary to exercise DUE DILIGENCE to verify that a user claiming to be an adult is in fact not a child, which is precisely why the Rules prescribe DigiLocker / virtual-token-based verification; a self-declaration checkbox is not due diligence. An 18+ gate therefore CREATES a verification obligation rather than removing one, the 2026 Gaming Rules are reported to impose age verification on online social games in their own right, and DPDP applies in full to adult users regardless. Phasing: rules 1, 2 and 17-21 from 13 November 2025 (Board constituted); Consent Manager registration from 13 November 2026; full substantive compliance from 13 May 2027. THIS REMAINS THE BIGGEST NON-GAMING COST FOR INDIA: the existing cohort/retention/session analytics would be unlawful as applied to minors.

checklist.item: Publish a DPDP-compliant consent notice, appoint a contact for data-principal grievances, and stand up breach-notification and data-erasure workflows
checklist.issuer: Data Protection Board of India
checklist.prerequisite: DPDP gap analysis
checklist.notes: Itemised, plain-language notice; consent withdrawal as easy as giving it; erasure on withdrawal. Significant Data Fiduciary designation (DPDP Act s.10; DPDP Rules 2025 rule 13, rule number UNVERIFIED) brings audits, algorithmic due diligence and possible restrictions on transferring specified personal data outside India — unlikely at launch scale but re-test on growth. CITATION CAVEAT (audit, contested): the prior version cited the DPDP Rules 2025 three times as "G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025". The G.S.R. number could not be corroborated from any source reached and the date is contested (Wikipedia gives 14 November 2025 for notification). Cite the Rules by name only until the gazette reference is checked.

checklist.item: If the product hosts ANY third-party content (chat, user profiles, user-submitted questions, leaderboard names), comply with IT Rules 2021 intermediary due diligence: publish rules/privacy policy/terms, appoint a Grievance Officer with Indian contact details, and meet the takedown and grievance timelines
checklist.issuer: MeitY
checklist.leadTime: In force now; 2021 Rules as amended — the Grievance Appellate Committee route has been live since October 2022, the latest amendments effective 20 February 2026
checklist.prerequisite: Determination of whether you are an "intermediary" at all
checklist.notes: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, as amended. A pure publisher app with no third-party content is NOT an intermediary — but it also has no s.79 safe harbour. CORRECTED (audit — misattribution): the prior version said the 2026 amendment "adds a Grievance Appellate Committee route with a 30-day user appeal window". IT DOES NOT. The Grievance Appellate Committee and the 30-day user appeal window were created by the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) AMENDMENT RULES, 2022 (rule 3A), in force since OCTOBER 2022 — four years earlier. Building to a 2026 baseline for the GAC would mis-date your compliance obligations by four years: the appeal route is already live and already applies to you. What the 2026 amendment (notified 10 February 2026, effective 20 February 2026) is confirmed to add: a 3-hour takedown for contempt/defamation-type categories, quarterly user notification, and labelling/metadata duties for synthetically generated (AI) content — relevant if any questions, art or voice are AI-generated. IMPORTANT: do NOT build to the 2023 "online gaming intermediary" / self-regulatory body regime (rules 4A/4B). No SRB was ever designated, the operative provisions never came into force, and PROG Act s.18 gives the Act overriding effect.

checklist.item: Scrub all advertising, app-store listing copy, influencer briefs and affiliate contracts of anything that promotes or induces money gaming
checklist.issuer: OGAI / MeitY; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: s.6 is a standalone offence: making, causing to be made, aiding, abetting or inducing any advertisement that "directly or indirectly promotes or induces any person to play any online money game". Penalty under s.9(2): up to 2 years or ₹50 lakh or both; repeat offences carry a minimum 2 years and minimum ₹50 lakh under s.9(5). Note s.10 makes only ss.5 and 7 cognizable and non-bailable — s.6 is not. Affiliates and influencers are caught in their own right, so indemnities alone are insufficient. Language like "stake", "bet", "pot", "escrow", "winnings" and "cash out" in India-facing copy invites a suo motu determination even for a lawful product — and it is precisely the evidence a regulator taking the aggressive reading of s.2(1)(j) would use against a purchased-coin duel.

checklist.item: Rewrite terms of service to state that coins have no monetary value, are non-transferable, non-redeemable, non-refundable in cash, and confer no property right
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; evidential before OGAI on the determination factors [RULE NUMBER INDICATIVE ONLY — 2026 Rules gazette text not obtained; secondary sources conflict]
checklist.prerequisite: Ledger decision
checklist.notes: The determination factors are reported to include whether rewards or in-game assets "can be transferred, redeemed, monetised or used outside the game environment". On the conjunctive construction of s.2(1)(j) this lane adopts, these terms are not just evidential — non-convertibility is the operative element of the defence. But terms are not a defence on their own: the architecture has to match them, and a live secondary market or an account-trading path defeats them regardless of what the terms say. Also cover subscription auto-renewal disclosure and cancellation under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.

checklist.item: Write and rehearse an India WIND-DOWN plan: what happens to Indian users' coin balances, in-flight duels and subscription entitlements the day a feature is geo-blocked or the app is delisted
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; consumer exposure under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
checklist.leadTime: Before India launch — not after a takedown
checklist.prerequisite: India launch decision
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION — missing entirely from the prior version, which described enforcement as delisting and payment cut-off "within days" and then gave no guidance on the aftermath. s.5 bites immediately and enforcement is intermediary-led, so the realistic scenario is that Indian users lose access overnight with unspent purchased balances and unresolved duels. Decide in advance: refund policy for unspent purchased currency, settlement rule for in-flight duels, pro-rata subscription refunds, chargeback handling and dispute volume, and consumer-protection exposure under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020. UNVERIFIED: the specific e-commerce-rules duties that would attach to a forced wind-down.

checklist.item: Check the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 and State prize-competition and lottery legislation before designing ANY free-entry, AMOE-style or skill-prize workaround
checklist.issuer: State governments; Central Government under the Prize Competitions Act, 1955
checklist.leadTime: Before designing any prize mechanic for India
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION. The prior version stated flatly that "there is no sweepstakes doctrine, no dual currency carve-out and no alternative method of entry defence anywhere in Indian law" and never mentioned the governing statutes. The correct statement is narrower and more useful: there is no PROGA carve-out for sweepstakes, dual currency or AMOE, AND the instruments that actually govern free-entry and skill-based prize competitions in India — the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 and State prize-competition/lottery legislation — CONSTRAIN such designs rather than enabling them. A US founder reaching for an AMOE redesign must clear both PROGA and this layer. UNVERIFIED: the scope of the 1955 Act as applied to an online quiz, and which State enactments bite; obtain a State-by-State view from Indian counsel if any prize mechanic is contemplated.

checklist.item: Choose the entity route: Indian private limited company, or foreign entity selling into India with an OIDAR registration and Indian representative
checklist.issuer: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) for Indian incorporation
checklist.prerequisite: Confirmed classification as an online social game
checklist.notes: FDI in "gambling and betting" is a prohibited sector under India's FDI policy / FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, so if the product were ever classified an online money game, foreign investment into an Indian operating entity would itself be unlawful — a strong reason to get the classification in writing before taking money, and a reason the CONTESTED purchased-coin question matters to your cap table and not only to your criminal exposure. A lawful online social game is an ordinary digital service for FDI purposes (100% automatic route) — confirm with counsel against the current consolidated FDI policy. Related open question (audit addition): whether a foreign provider with no Indian presence can file a determination application at all, and what a point-of-contact / India-resident-officer requirement would do to that — UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: Run a permanent-establishment / significant economic presence analysis before scaling India revenue
checklist.issuer: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
checklist.leadTime: Before crossing India revenue or user thresholds
checklist.prerequisite: India revenue forecast
checklist.notes: Significant Economic Presence under s.9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Explanation 2A) creates a business connection in India for a non-resident above revenue or user thresholds prescribed by Rule 11UD of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. THE THRESHOLD FIGURES ARE UNVERIFIED — do not plan against remembered numbers. Treaty relief may apply depending on the entity's residence. The 2% equalisation levy on e-commerce supply was withdrawn; confirm current position with counsel.

checklist.item: Treat the CURRENT FREE PRODUCT as in-scope for India now — do not defer India work until monetisation
checklist.issuer: OGAI / MeitY; Data Protection Board of India
checklist.leadTime: Now, if the free product has Indian users
checklist.prerequisite: Indian users of the existing free build
checklist.notes: AUDIT ADDITION — CORRECTS A FRAMING ERROR THAT RUNS THROUGH THE PRIOR VERSION. The prior version repeatedly called the existing free product "safe" and said India obligations begin "at the first rupee". That is right on the GAMING-OFFENCE analysis only: free-minted, non-convertible coins are not "other stakes" and no money game is offered. It is wrong as a statement about India obligations generally. Two regimes attach to a free product with Indian users: (a) the 2026 Rules' social-game safeguards (age verification, parental controls, time limits, fair play, grievance) — UNVERIFIED as to scope, see the dedicated item; and (b) the DPDP child-data regime, which applies to the existing cohort/retention/session analytics as applied to Indian minors irrespective of whether any money changes hands. Audit and remediate the free build's India posture now.

checklist.item: Obtain a written India opinion from Indian counsel before enabling any real-money flow, and re-test after the Supreme Court rules
checklist.issuer: Indian counsel (gaming/technology practice)
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec and ledger architecture
checklist.notes: THIS IS A COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST, NOT LEGAL ADVICE. The points that genuinely need local counsel, in priority order: (1) THE CONTESTED QUESTION — whether purchased, non-cashable coins staked player-v-player are "other stakes" under s.2(1)(j), and whether the "monetary and other enrichment" conjunction in s.2(1)(g) helps; (2) whether the 2026 Rules impose age-verification, parental-control, time-limit, fair-play and grievance duties on online social games, and whether registration triggers India data residency — both UNVERIFIED here and both cost-bearing; (3) whether cosmetic loot boxes / randomised rewards survive the determination factors in OGAI's hands; (4) whether you are an "intermediary" for IT Rules purposes; (5) the FDI characterisation; (6) SEP/PE exposure; (7) whether an 18+ gate with real verification or verifiable parental consent is the cheaper DPDP path for your funnel — noting that the gate is NOT an exit from verification; (8) whether a foreign entity with no Indian presence can file a determination application, and the exposure of doing so.

risks: THE DECISIVE OPEN QUESTION (RESTATED AFTER AUDIT): whether purchased, NON-CASHABLE coins staked player-v-player constitute an "online money game". The prior version of this lane asserted as fact that they do, and that the escrow duel "flips from lawful to criminal" the instant coins become purchasable. THAT ASSERTION IS WITHDRAWN. The point is genuinely unsettled: no OGAI determination, no judgment, and reasonable Indian counsel differ. The permissive reading (conjunctive s.2(1)(j): the thing must be BOTH convertible to money AND purchased) is supported by the most directly on-point published 2026 analysis and by the "monetary AND other enrichment" conjunction in s.2(1)(g). The restrictive reading is available on the words and is the one a policy-minded regulator would reach for. The RISK is the unquantifiability, not a known answer — and it sits in a regime where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable.

Criminal, personal and non-bailable. s.10 makes ss.5 and 7 cognizable and non-bailable; s.11 makes anyone "in charge of, and responsible to, the company for the conduct of that part of the business" liable, plus any consenting/conniving director, manager, secretary or officer (independent and non-executive directors not in actual decision-making are carved out); s.16 permits entry and search of "any place, whether physical or digital", arrest without warrant, and overriding of access controls. This is not a regulatory-fine regime. It is also why a contested construction should be bought out with engineering (two ledgers) rather than argued about after launch.

Extraterritorial reach is explicit. s.1(2): the Act "applies to online money gaming service offered within the territory of India or operated from outside the territory of India". The long title names services operating "from foreign jurisdictions". Incorporating in Delaware or Dublin does not put Models B or C outside the Act — it only changes the enforcement route to blocking, delisting and payment cut-off.

Enforcement is fast and intermediary-led, not court-led — and the appeal happens afterwards. OGAI became operational on 1 May 2026 and issued its first advisory on 29 July 2026 to app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos, banks, social media intermediaries, OTT platforms and advertising agencies, citing ss.5, 6 and 7. 8,376 betting/gambling URLs had been blocked as of 28 March 2026, over 4,800 of them after the Act. Expect removal from Indian app storefronts and payment refusal within days of a complaint. CORRECTED (audit): there IS an appeal route — reported as the Secretary, MeitY as Appellate Authority, 30 days to file and 30 days for disposal, then High Court writ jurisdiction. The prior version wrongly said the appellate tier had been dropped and left the founder with no remedy. Identify the route before you need it.

The blocking power's relationship to s.69A of the IT Act 2000 is CONTESTED. The prior version asserted that s.14 permits blocking "notwithstanding s.69A". That is UNVERIFIED — the provision was not quoted. Whether s.14 overrides s.69A or operates through it and the 2009 Blocking Rules determines whether the s.69A procedural safeguards (committee, hearing, reasoned order) attach to a blocking order against the app. Material to any contingency plan.

The Supreme Court challenge is pending and there is NO stay. Head Digital Works v Union of India, T.C.(C) No. 133/2025, before a three-judge bench of CJI Surya Kant, J. Joymalya Bagchi and J. V.M. Pancholi; High Court petitions transferred under Article 139A in September 2025; hearings ran through 2026 with a listing on 5 August 2026; no judgment found as at 14 September 2026. The Act came into force on 1 May 2026 notwithstanding the challenge. Plan on the Act standing; a favourable judgment would be upside, not a basis for launching now.

Classification can be revisited at any time and OGAI can determine SUO MOTU. Determinations are reported to bind only your product and only while the model is unchanged; any move toward staking is a material change triggering reclassification, cessation directions, advertising prohibition and blocking. Rule numbers for this machinery are INDICATIVE ONLY (see corrections).

Social-casino and loot-box mechanics are the live policy debate, and a purchased-coin duel is at its centre. Indian commentary in 2026 openly describes cosmetic-currency games as exposing a "loophole" in PROGA — real money in, no cash out, casino psychology. Note the two-sidedness: the same commentary that calls it a loophole concludes it is currently LAWFUL. A loophole is a thing that works until it is closed. MeitY can notify a category of online social games into MANDATORY registration at any time, and the reward-monetisation determination factor gives OGAI a hook. A randomised-reward cosmetic economy in a game with duel framing remains the highest-scrutiny design you could ship into India.

Oversight of social games is complaint-driven — which cuts both ways. There is no pre-clearance requirement, so you can ship without approval; but a competitor, a parent or a consumer group can trigger a suo motu determination, and your first contact with OGAI will then be adversarial rather than a voluntary application you controlled. Weigh that against the disclosed costs of filing voluntarily (data residency, regulator exposure, eligibility uncertainty).

AFFIRMATIVE DUTIES ON THE LAWFUL MODELS ARE A REAL AND LARGELY UNMAPPED COST (audit addition). The 2026 Rules are reported to impose age verification, parental controls, time limits, fair-play monitoring and grievance redressal on online social games generally — i.e. on Models A and D and on the current free product. I could not corroborate the scope from the sources reachable and the gazette text was not obtained. The risk is that a founder treats "lawful" as "unregulated" and ships with no age gate, no parental controls and no grievance officer.

DPDP's under-18 rules are a product constraint, not a policy document — and an 18+ gate is not an escape. Everyone under 18 is a child; s.9(3) prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children and consent cannot cure it (though s.9(4) permits Government-prescribed exemptions, unlikely to reach a quiz game); penalties reach ₹200 crore for s.9 breaches and ₹250 crore for security-safeguard failures. The DPDP Rules 2025 require due diligence that an adult claimant is not a child, so a self-declared 18+ checkbox creates an obligation rather than removing one. Existing cohort/retention/session analytics and any personalised question-difficulty or ad targeting would be unlawful as applied to Indian minors. Compliance bites 13 May 2027.

App-store policy is a second, independent gate. Apple and Google separately restrict real-money gaming apps in India to licensed operators — and with PROGA there is no licence to hold. Even a lawful Model A/D build can be caught by over-broad store review if the listing copy uses staking language. Store review is also the fastest enforcement channel against you.

State law has NOT been mapped away (audit addition). The Public Gambling Act, 1867 and State adaptations still govern offline activity; Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana legislated against online gaming before PROGA; and the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 plus State prize-competition and lottery legislation govern free-entry and skill-prize competitions — the very design space a US founder would reach for as an AMOE workaround. s.18 gives PROGA overriding effect to the extent of INCONSISTENCY, which is not the same as extinguishing additional State duties. The prior version's statement that no such doctrine exists anywhere in Indian law is withdrawn.

Advertising liability attaches to people you do not control. s.6 catches anyone who makes, causes to be made, aids, abets or induces a money-gaming advertisement — affiliates, influencers, ad networks and celebrity endorsers in their own right. Contractual indemnities do not remove their criminal exposure or the reputational blast radius.

WIND-DOWN EXPOSURE (audit addition). If a feature is geo-blocked or the app delisted, Indian users lose access overnight holding unspent purchased balances, in-flight duels and live subscriptions. Refunds, chargebacks and consumer-protection exposure under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 are unmodelled. Decide the policy before launch.

common.item: Decide the product model BEFORE opening any merchant account, and never describe the business to a processor in terms that trip the prohibited list ('stake', 'wager', 'prize', 'cash out', 'escrow', 'winner takes the pot')
common.issuer: Internal / Stripe, Adyen, PayPal, Paddle underwriting
common.notes: Underwriting is done on your own copy, so the words the product uses are a real underwriting input. AUDIT CORRECTION — the brief's original claim that FACT//DUEL's live UI 'already uses stake, escrow and winner takes the escrow' is withdrawn as fabricated. Verified by grep across the working tree (node_modules and .git excluded): the phrase 'winner takes the escrow' appears in NO product code — its only occurrences are inside this project's own compliance and research documents (docs/money/*, public/product/compliance/*), which quote the brief itself. 'escrow' appears ZERO times in app/ and components/ (the entire UI layer); it exists only as an internal server-side field in lib/server/room-engine.mjs (r.escrow, r.balances[winner] += r.escrow) and in tests. 'stake' occurs ~55 times in app/ and components/ but overwhelmingly as CSS class names and prop/identifier names (fd-exp-stake-line, stake-label, config.stake); the user-visible strings at those sites are neutral ('Entry · once per match', 'Free entry', 'N coins'). So the exposure is much smaller than the brief asserted and there is no shipped, indexable prohibited-category copy. The remedial action still stands and is cheap: before filing any merchant application, rename the internal escrow/stake concepts and keep user-facing copy in entry/reward language, and make sure the compliance documents themselves are not published at a public URL under the company's own domain where an underwriter would read them as a description of the business. Misdescribing the business to a processor remains a termination-plus-clawback event under every processor agreement, so the fix is to change the product, not the wording.

common.item: Stripe standard account for coin purchases (closed-loop, non-redeemable) and for subscriptions
common.cost: 2.9% + $0.30 per successful domestic US card charge (stripe.com/pricing, fetched 14 Sep 2026); +1.5% international cards, +1% currency conversion
common.leadTime: UNVERIFIED (self-serve onboarding is same-day; underwriting review varies)
common.prerequisite: Legal entity, bank account, beneficial-owner KYC
common.notes: Lawful and supported ONLY while the coin is a true one-way closed-loop token: no cash-out, no redemption for anything of monetary value, no player-versus-player staking. Model A and D are ordinary digital-goods commerce. AUDIT CAVEAT — absence from Stripe's prohibited and restricted lists is not an affirmative approval of a virtual-currency model; acquirers commonly carry a stored-value / virtual-currency restriction independent of their gambling lines (Paddle's does exactly this and kills Model A outright). Describe the coin accurately at onboarding as a non-redeemable in-game entitlement and get the category acceptance confirmed in writing rather than inferred from a silent list.

common.item: Do NOT attempt Stripe for Models B or C — there is no pre-approval path
common.cost: n/a
common.notes: Stripe's Prohibited and Restricted Businesses list (last updated 13 May 2026) places in the PROHIBITED column: 'Games of chance including gambling, internet gambling, casino games, sweepstakes and contests, and fantasy sports leagues with a monetary or material prize'; 'Games of skill including video game and mobile game tournaments or competitions, darts, card games, and board games with a monetary or material prize'; and 'Payments of an entry or player fee that promise the entrant or player will win a prize of value'. That third line is a verbatim description of Model C. Restricted-list categories can be pre-approved; PROHIBITED ones cannot. AUDIT CORRECTION — the brief presented 'regardless of local legality' as a verbatim Stripe quotation; that phrase could not be confirmed as text on support.stripe.com's prohibited-business FAQ and is withdrawn as a quote. The SUBSTANCE is sound and is retained unquoted: the FAQ answers 'Internet gambling is legal in my region, so why was my application rejected?' by pointing to Stripe's own processor and financial-partner obligations, i.e. local legality does not by itself make the category acceptable. The adjacent phrase 'games of skill (or chance) with cash prizes, sweepstakes, pay-in auctions' IS verbatim and may be quoted. Do not reproduce the withdrawn phrase inside quotation marks in anything filed or shown to counsel.

common.item: Adyen direct merchant account with written waiver for 'Legal gambling or Game of Skill'
common.cost: UNVERIFIED (Adyen is interchange++ with a per-transaction processing fee; no published gaming rate)
common.prerequisite: CONTESTED: the brief stated 'gambling or skill-gaming licence in each target market' as the prerequisite. That is an inference, not published Adyen text, and for Model C it may be unsatisfiable — see notes. Plus enhanced onboarding documentation and Adyen's written waiver, granted at Adyen's sole discretion.
common.notes: Adyen's Prohibited and Restricted list (last updated 13 Nov 2025) marks 'Legal gambling or Game of Skill where participants receive cash or cash equivalents or prizes with/of material value: including but not limited to: Casinos, poker, bingo, slot machines, betting, lotteries, racing, fantasy sports' as RESTRICTED for direct merchants (waiver possible, revocable at Adyen's sole discretion) but PROHIBITED for platform/partner businesses. CRITICAL: 'Any type of US based gambling services' is in Adyen's PROHIBITED column outright — so Adyen is an EU/UK rail for Models B and C, never a US one. AUDIT ADDITION — the 'Adyen route' for Model C may be ILLUSORY rather than merely slow. Adyen's category word is 'Legal gambling', which implies a licensed operator. But in the UK a paid-entry prize competition decided by genuine skill, knowledge or judgement sits OUTSIDE the Gambling Commission's licensing regime entirely — there is no skill-contest licence to obtain (secondary: UK practitioner commentary on Gambling Act 2005 prize competitions; not verified against Gambling Commission primary text). If Adyen's underwriting requires a licence the applicant cannot obtain because no such licence category exists, the waiver prerequisite is unsatisfiable and Model C has no mainstream EU/UK rail either. UNVERIFIED and decision-critical: put this question to Adyen underwriting in writing BEFORE building any Model C checkout — 'what evidence of lawfulness do you accept for a paid-entry skill contest in a jurisdiction that issues no licence for it?'

common.item: Do NOT use Paddle or Lemon Squeezy for coin sales in any model
common.issuer: Paddle.com Market Ltd (Paddle owns Lemon Squeezy)
common.cost: n/a
common.notes: Paddle's Acceptable Use Policy (last updated 13 April 2026) prohibits 'Virtual currency or stored value, including but not limited to store credit, gift cards, vouchers' — this kills even Model A's coin purchase, not just the gambling models. It separately prohibits 'lotteries, auctions, contests, sweepstakes, or games of chance', 'Betting-related products, competition/event tickets, or entries', fantasy sports, money transfer services, and marketplaces. Paddle does run a 'Paddle for games' product, but for game and DLC licences, not in-game currency.

common.item: Paddle / merchant-of-record for the SUBSCRIPTION only (Model D)
common.issuer: Paddle, FastSpring, Polar or similar MoR
common.cost: UNVERIFIED (Paddle's published headline is a percentage-plus-fixed reseller fee; confirm current rate card)
common.notes: A recurring fee for features and cosmetics with no stake and no prize is squarely inside every MoR's acceptable use. This is the only model where the MoR route is clean.

common.item: Understand precisely what merchant-of-record does and does not move
common.notes: MoR MOVES: the card-scheme merchant relationship and chargeback liability; PCI-DSS merchant scope (the MoR hosts checkout); sales-tax/VAT/GST registration, collection, remittance and invoicing in ~100 jurisdictions; the consumer-contract counterparty and refund obligation. MoR DOES NOT MOVE: gambling or gaming licensing — the licensable act is OFFERING the game, which is you, not the reseller; money transmission — if you hold a user balance and pay it out, that is your activity and no MoR touches it; KYC/AML on payouts; age assurance inside the game; the underlying legality of the stake. Decisive practical point: MoRs are a ONE-WAY pay-in rail. None of Paddle, FastSpring or Lemon Squeezy does player payouts. For Models B and C the payout half — the hard, regulated half — is entirely unserved by MoR.

common.item: PayPal / Braintree — treat as unavailable for B and C without explicit pre-approval
common.issuer: PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. / PayPal, Inc. / Braintree
common.cost: n/a
common.prerequisite: Pre-approval; demonstrated ability to block gambling for US account holders and any jurisdiction where it may be illegal
common.notes: PayPal's Acceptable Use Policy prohibits gambling — 'placing, accepting, recording, or registering bets... or otherwise carrying on a game of chance for money, property, or other things of value' — absent pre-approval, and PayPal's help content states approval requires satisfying PayPal that you can block US account holders. Secondary sources (SeamlessChex, July 2026) report holding a recognised gaming licence does not by itself lift the restriction. PayPal is fine for Models A and D as ordinary digital goods.

common.item: Gambling-specialist acquirer / PSP (licence-gated)
common.issuer: Worldpay (FIS), Nuvei, Paysafe (Skrill/Neteller), Trustly, PayNearMe, Praxis Tech — vendor list is indicative, from trade knowledge not a fetched source
common.cost: UNVERIFIED — expect a markedly higher discount rate than 2.9%, a rolling reserve, and a minimum monthly volume
common.prerequisite: Gambling/gaming licence in each market; MCC 7995 registration; card-network high-integrity-risk programme registration
common.notes: This is the only realistic rail for a cash-redeemable stake product. Every one of them requires the licence first, so the payments workstream cannot start until the licensing workstream is finished. UNVERIFIED: MCC 7995 assignment rules and Visa/Mastercard high-integrity-risk registration fees were not verified in this research — confirm with the acquirer.

common.item: Apple: use StoreKit in-app purchase for coin sales in Model A and subscriptions in Model D
common.cost: AUDIT ADDITION (the brief left the dominant cost line blank). Apple standard commission 30%; App Store Small Business Program 15% for developers with up to USD 1,000,000 in prior-calendar-year proceeds across all their apps, and for developers new to the App Store — secondary but well corroborated (Apple Developer SBP page and multiple 2026 practitioner summaries); not fetched from Apple's own schedule in this pass, so re-confirm on the Apple Developer site before modelling. EU alternative business terms under the DMA are reported at a reduced rate (13% figure reported, UNVERIFIED). US external-purchase-link commission rates are in flux following Epic v. Apple and are UNVERIFIED.
common.notes: App Store Review Guideline 3.1.1 requires IAP to unlock 'in-game currencies'. Two traps: (a) 'Any credits or in-game currencies purchased via in-app purchase may not expire' — so coin balances cannot be time-expired; (b) if you ever ship randomised rewards, 3.1.1 requires disclosing the odds of each item type before purchase.

common.item: Apple: Model B cannot sell its stake currency through IAP — this is a hard block, not a review-risk
common.cost: n/a
common.notes: Guideline 5.3.3 verbatim: 'Apps may not use in-app purchase to purchase credit or currency for use in conjunction with real money gaming of any kind.' Guideline 5.3.4: real-money-gaming apps 'must have necessary licensing and permissions in the locations where the app is used, must be geo-restricted to those locations, and must be free on the App Store.' Combined effect: on iOS a Model B app must be free, licensed, geofenced, and must fund balances OUTSIDE IAP via a web top-up. CONTESTED (audit, possible) — the brief also warned that 'the historic Guideline 4.7.1 real-money-gaming restriction has been removed'. The second half of that warning is right and is retained: current 4.7 covers 'Mini apps, mini games, streaming games, chatbots, plug-ins, and game emulators' and current 4.7.1 concerns privacy compliance, moderation/reporting mechanisms and Guideline 3.1 conformity for digital goods. But the auditor could not confirm that a real-money-gaming restriction ever sat at 4.7.1 — Apple's real-money gaming and sweepstakes rules have lived at 5.3 for years. Treat the claimed citation history as UNVERIFIED and do not repeat it to counsel; the operative point is simply that 5.3, not 4.7, is where real-money gaming lives today.

common.item: Apple: if Model B or C funds balances off-app, build the web top-up flow and rely on the US-storefront link-out carve-out
common.cost: UNVERIFIED (US external-link commission rate not fetched)
common.prerequisite: Apple Developer Program; for non-US storefronts, a StoreKit External Purchase Link Entitlement
common.notes: Guideline 3.1.1(a) now states entitlements 'are not required for developers to include buttons, external links, or other calls to action in their United States storefront apps', and that the anti-steering prohibition applies 'In all other storefronts, except for the United States storefront, where this prohibition does not apply'. So a US-storefront app may link out to a web wallet top-up freely; EU and other storefronts need the External Purchase Link Entitlement. India follows the general rule.

common.item: Google Play: complete the gambling-app application and hold a licence per country/state for Model B
common.cost: UNVERIFIED
